0.title: The Sound Church: Titus and the Gospel-Ordered Life
0.overview:
Titus is the most compressed of the three Pastoral Epistles — three chapters of extraordinary density that move from theology to character to conduct without pausing. Paul writes to Titus, his Greek co-worker and 'true child in a common faith,' whom he has left on Crete with a single, sprawling assignment: 'put what remained into order, and appoint elders in every town' (1:5). The churches of Crete are young, disorganized, and under pressure from teachers who combine Jewish speculative traditions with moral permissiveness. Titus's task is to build a church that looks like the gospel it proclaims.

Crete was one of the ancient world's most storied islands — home to a hundred cities, to the legendary palace of Knossos and the Minoan civilization, and to a reputation for unreliability so notorious it had become proverbial in antiquity. The Cretan philosopher Epimenides (c. 6th century BC) had declared that 'Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons,' a statement Paul quotes in 1:12 without embarrassment — cultural honesty is not racism, and the false teachers have confirmed the description. Paul and Titus had apparently visited Crete together at some point unrecorded in Acts (probably during the period between Paul's first and second Roman imprisonments), planted churches across the island, and then Paul left Titus to complete the work while he moved on.

The letter's organizing principle is the word 'sound' — hygiainō (healthy, health-giving). Sound doctrine (1:9; 2:1), sound faith (1:13; 2:2), sound speech (2:8) are the letter's repeated standard. The false teachers produce diseased teaching — teaching that makes people spiritually sick. Sound doctrine, by contrast, produces healthy congregations: older men of dignity, older women who form the younger, young people of self-control, slaves whose conduct adorns the gospel. The letter is a sustained argument that right belief and right living are inseparable — that the grace of God which saves also trains; that the gospel is not just good news about forgiveness but the power that produces a 'people for his own possession, eager for good works' (2:14).

Two Christological passages make Titus indispensable for preaching the full person of Christ. In 2:13 the Greek grammar (Sharp's Rule) identifies Jesus Christ as 'our great God and Savior' — one of the New Testament's most explicit affirmations of full deity. In 3:4–7 the paragraph on regeneration, justification, and Spirit-renewal is one of the most complete soteriological statements in Paul's letters, anchoring the call to godly conduct in the deepest possible theological foundation: God saved us not because of what we did but entirely by his own mercy, through the Spirit's renewing, so that we might become heirs of the hope of eternal life. The letter that sounds like a manual of church order is, at its root, a profound meditation on grace.

1.title: The Ordered Church: Elders, Sound Doctrine, and False Teachers
1.overview:
Paul left Titus on Crete to finish organising the young churches. Chapter 1 has three parts: a long greeting that grounds everything in the God who cannot lie (vv. 1–4); the qualifications of elders, who must be men of proven character able to teach and to refute (vv. 5–9); and a sharp word about false teachers, mostly from the circumcision party, who teach for money (vv. 10–16).

The elders are defined by the threat, and the false teachers are exposed by the standard: truth “accords with godliness” (v. 1).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before a word of instruction, Paul sets out where the truth comes from: the eternal promise of a God who cannot lie, revealed in history and entrusted to a preacher. Then a greeting to a Greek son in a shared faith.
verseByVerse.theology:
The God Who Cannot Lie, Writing to Crete

Apseudes, the unlying God (v. 2), is the first thing Paul says about God to an island proverbial for lying (v. 12); and the eternal promise reaches anyone only through preaching entrusted to a man (v. 3).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Titus was the uncircumcised test case at Jerusalem (Galatians 2:1–3) and the man sent into the Corinthian crisis (2 Corinthians 7:6).

Now: Knowledge of the truth is recognised by the godliness it produces (v. 1).

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ, for the sake of the faith of God's elect and their knowledge of the truth, which accords with godliness, in hope of eternal life, which God, who never lies, promised before the ages began and at the proper time manifested in his word through the preaching with which I have been entrusted by the command of God our Savior;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ, for the sake of the faith of God’s elect and their knowledge of the truth, which accords with godliness, in hope of eternal life, which God, who never lies, promised before the ages began and at the proper time manifested in his word through the preaching with which I have been entrusted by the command of God our Savior;

Meaning first. Titus 1 is about order in young churches threatened by false teachers. Paul’s unusually full greeting sums up his ministry: he serves the faith of God’s chosen people and their knowledge of the truth that produces godliness, resting on the hope of eternal life promised by the God who cannot lie (vv. 1–4). He left Titus in Crete to set the churches in order and appoint elders in every town (v. 5): men above reproach at home and in character, holding firmly to the trustworthy message so that they can teach sound doctrine and refute those who oppose it (vv. 6–9). This was urgent, because deceivers, especially from the circumcision party, were upsetting whole households for money (vv. 10–11). A Cretan poet had called Cretans liars, beasts and gluttons; Titus must rebuke them sharply, so that they become sound in the faith (vv. 12–14). The false teachers, defiled in mind and conscience, claim to know God while denying him by their deeds (vv. 15–16). Over the whole chapter stands the first thing Paul says about God: he never lies.

The setting. Titus was a Greek convert and one of Paul’s trusted troubleshooters. Paul had taken him, uncircumcised, to Jerusalem as a test case for the gospel’s freedom (Galatians 2:1–5), and sent him to Corinth to deal with a crisis and organise the collection (2 Corinthians 2:13; 7:6–15; 8:6, 16–23). After Paul’s release from his first Roman imprisonment, the two evangelised Crete, a large island south of Greece, and Paul left Titus there to organise the churches, writing this letter around AD 63–65. Later Titus went to Dalmatia (2 Timothy 4:10). Cretans were present at Pentecost (Acts 2:11), so there may have been believers there before Paul arrived.

An unusually long opening. For so short a letter the opening sentence is remarkably long, and the length is the point. Titus is going to face people on Crete who claim superior knowledge, and before a word of instruction Paul sets out, in three verses, where the truth actually comes from: from the eternal purpose of a God who cannot lie, revealed in history, and handed to a preacher.

Paul, a servant of God. “Servant” (doulos) means slave. Only here does Paul call himself a servant of God; elsewhere he is a servant of Christ Jesus. The title places him in line with Moses, David and the prophets, the servants of the LORD (Joshua 1:2; Jeremiah 7:25). It is the lowest word in the Roman household and the highest title in Israel’s Scriptures, and Paul wears both meanings at once.

And an apostle of Jesus Christ. Servant expresses humility; apostle expresses authority. The combination, God’s slave and Christ’s apostle, appears nowhere else in Paul, and the pairing is deliberate in a letter that will call both Father and Son our Saviour within four verses.

For the sake of the faith of God’s elect. “For the sake of” (kata) means in accordance with, with a view to. Paul’s apostleship exists to bring God’s elect to faith and to build up their faith. “Elect” (eklektōn) means chosen ones. God chose a people; Paul preaches so that they will believe (2 Timothy 2:10; Acts 13:48). Election does not make preaching unnecessary; it guarantees its success.

Election comes first. God’s elect are those God has chosen for salvation, and Paul’s whole ministry serves their faith. Arminian Christians (named after the Dutch teacher Jacob Arminius) hold that God chose those he foresaw would believe; they love and preach the gospel, and the question is how to read texts like these. But Paul says the hope of eternal life was promised before the ages began (v. 2), and elsewhere that God saved us not because of our works but because of his own purpose and grace, given us in Christ Jesus before the ages began (2 Timothy 1:9). The more likely reading is that election comes first and faith is its fruit. The doctrine is not a reason to sit still. It is the reason a missionary can land on an island of liars and expect a church.

And their knowledge of the truth, which accords with godliness. “Knowledge” (epignōsis) means full knowledge, knowing that has taken hold. “Accords with godliness” (kat’ eusebeian) means leads to godliness, fits with it. Truth is recognised by the life it produces. A knowledge that leaves a man unchanged has failed the definition, whatever its content, and the false teachers on Crete had exactly that: knowledge without godliness (v. 16).

In hope of eternal life. “Hope” (elpis) is confident expectation, not wishful thinking. Faith, knowledge and godliness all rest on the hope of eternal life (3:7). The Christian is not godly in order to earn a future; he is godly because a future has been promised to him and is certain.

Which God, who never lies, promised before the ages began. “Who never lies” (apseudēs) is a single word, the unlying God, and it occurs only here in the New Testament. Now recall where this letter is going: Crete, whose reputation was summed up in the line Paul quotes in verse 12, Cretans are always liars. The first thing he says about God, in a letter to an island proverbial for deceit, is that he cannot lie (Numbers 23:19; Hebrews 6:18). Before the ages began (pro chronōn aiōniōn) is the same phrase as 2 Timothy 1:9. The promise was made before there was anyone to make it to. It was made in eternity, within the Trinity: the Father promised eternal life to the elect in Christ, before creation. This is sometimes called the covenant of redemption. That is, before anything was made, the Father, the Son and the Spirit agreed together on our rescue, the Father giving a people to the Son, and the Son undertaking to come and lay down his life for them (John 6:37–39; 17:2, 6).

And at the proper time manifested in his word through the preaching. “At the proper time” (kairois idiois) means in his own seasons, as in 1 Timothy 2:6. “Manifested” (ephanerōsen) means made visible, revealed. “Preaching” (kērygma) means proclamation. What God promised in eternity, he revealed in history through the preached gospel.

The life that was with the Father. What exactly was promised before the ages and then brought into the open? John answers in almost the same terms: the eternal life, which was with the Father and was made manifest to us (1 John 1:2). The eternal life promised to the elect is not a thing apart from Christ. It was given us in Christ Jesus before the ages began (2 Timothy 1:9), and whoever has the Son has life (1 John 5:12). So the manifesting at the proper time was not only a sermon but a birth, a cross and an empty tomb, which the preaching announces. All the promises of God find their Yes in him (2 Corinthians 1:20).

With which I have been entrusted by the command of God our Saviour. “Entrusted” (episteuthēn), as in 1 Timothy 1:11: the deposit word again. An eternal promise, revealed at the right hour, and then handed to a man to announce. That is how it reaches anybody, which is why appointing the right men in every town, in verse 5, is not administration but the survival of the thing. God our Saviour (1 Timothy 1:1) is one of six Saviour titles in this short letter: three times the Father is God our Saviour (1:3; 2:10; 3:4), and three times Christ is our Saviour (1:4; 2:13; 3:6), once as our great God and Saviour.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul preached only to people he knew to be elect. He did not know who they were; he preached to all, knowing God would call his own through it. Nor does promised before the ages began mean anyone existed before time; it means God’s saving plan was fixed in eternity.

If God has chosen his elect, why should I share the gospel? Because God has chosen to save his elect through the gospel being shared. Election decides who will be saved; preaching is how they are reached. Paul endured everything for the sake of the elect, that they also may obtain salvation (2 Timothy 2:10). You do not know who the elect are, and you do not need to. Speak to everyone, pray for everyone, and trust God to open the hearts he has chosen to open, as he opened Lydia’s (Acts 16:14). Far from discouraging evangelism, election is its great encouragement: your words are not wasted, because God has a people and he will call them.

How can I know if I am one of God’s elect? Not by trying to look into God’s secret decrees, but by looking to Christ. The elect are those who come to Christ in faith, and whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37). If you trust Christ as your Saviour, love him, and want to follow him, that is the evidence that God chose you, because no one comes unless the Father draws him (John 6:44). If you are unsure, do not sit and wait to discover whether you are chosen; come to Christ now. Election is a doctrine for believers to rejoice in, not a barrier for seekers to stumble over.

In a sentence. Before Titus faces a single false teacher, Paul grounds everything in a God who cannot lie: he promised eternal life to his chosen people before time began, revealed it in Christ, and now spreads it through preaching that produces faith and godly lives.

In everyday life. Most lies are small and social: the excuse for being late, the story improved in the telling, the flattering answer. They seem harmless, but they are the Cretan habit in modern dress. A person who belongs to the God who never lies is free to be plainly truthful, and to let a yes be yes.

For worship. On an island where a man’s word was worth little, the God who cannot lie had kept his word for longer than there had been islands. He gave it before the ages began, when no one yet existed to hear it. He held to it through the fall, the flood, the exile and four silent centuries, and he kept it at last at the cost of his own Son’s life. Nothing he has ever said to his people has needed to be taken back. His faithfulness is older than the world and will outlast it, and every one of his chosen, on Crete or anywhere, stands on a word that has never once been broken.
verseByVerse.note: Titus was a Greek convert and one of Paul’s trusted troubleshooters. The letter was probably written between Paul’s two Roman imprisonments, in the mid 60s AD.

verseByVerse.quote: To Titus, my true child in a common faith: Grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To Titus, my true child in a common faith: Grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior.

To Titus, my true child. “True” (gnēsios) means genuine, legitimate, the real article, the same word used of Timothy (1 Timothy 1:2). Titus was probably converted through Paul. He is Paul’s authorised representative.

Who Titus was. A Greek and uncircumcised, he went with Paul to Jerusalem as a living test case and was not forced to be circumcised (Galatians 2:1–3): the exhibit in the argument over whether Gentiles could be Christians without becoming Jews. He was also the man Paul sent into the worst of the Corinthian crisis, and whose return with good news comforted him (2 Corinthians 7:6, 13–15). Where Timothy seems to have needed steadying, Titus gets the hard postings. Paul has now left him on Crete.

In a common faith. “Common” (koinos) means shared, held in partnership. Paul the Jew and Titus the Gentile share one faith. There is not one faith for Jews and another for Gentiles, and the apostle and his delegate are not on different tiers of Christianity. They hold the same faith on the same terms. This was significant in a church troubled by the circumcision party (v. 10).

Grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Saviour. Here Christ is called Saviour, just after the Father is called Saviour (v. 3). The same title is given to both. The interchange is not careless. Christ is the Saviour along with the Father, which places him on the side of deity, and Paul will make the argument explicit at 2:13, where he calls him our great God and Saviour.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts add mercy, reading grace, mercy and peace, matching 1 and 2 Timothy. The earlier manuscripts have only grace and peace. The shorter reading is very probably what Paul wrote, and the addition looks like a copyist bringing Titus into line with the letters to Timothy.

What it does not mean. Common does not mean ordinary or inferior; it means shared by all believers alike.

What does it mean to be someone’s child in the faith? It describes the bond between a believer and the person God used to bring him to Christ or to nurture him in his early years. It is a real family tie, and it carries love, gratitude and responsibility on both sides. It does not mean the spiritual father owns or controls the child; Titus is sent off to lead on his own. And you do not need to be an apostle to have one. A parent, a Sunday school teacher, a friend who explained the gospel, a pastor who walked with you: many believers have someone like that. Thank God for them, and ask him to let you be that for someone else.

In a sentence. A Jewish apostle and a Greek convert are father and son in one shared faith, and both receive grace and peace from the Father and from Christ, each rightly called Saviour.

In everyday life. In most churches there is someone whose background could hardly be further from yours, and yet you hold exactly the same faith on exactly the same terms. That is not a small thing; it is the gospel made visible. And somewhere there is a person who first brought you the faith, who may never have heard what came of it.

For worship. Grace and peace come from two persons who are one God: the Father who planned our salvation and the Son who accomplished it, both rightly called our Saviour. They have made a Jew and a Greek into father and son, and joined Gentiles from every island and city into one household by one faith. There is no second-class place in it. Every believer holds the same faith on the same terms, because every believer has the same Saviour, and he gave himself for all of them alike.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–9 — Appointing Elders in Every Town
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The churches of Crete are to be set in order by the right leaders: men whose homes and character are above reproach, who hold the apostles’ teaching firmly enough to feed the flock and guard it.
verseByVerse.theology:
Elder and Overseer Are One Office

‘Elders’ (v. 5) and ‘overseer’ (v. 7) name one office within a single sentence; and of the qualifications, eleven concern character and one competence: to instruct and to rebuke (v. 9).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Congregations existed across Crete without yet being in working order (v. 5).

Now: ‘Children are believers’ (v. 6), or ‘faithful’, asks whether a household is visibly out of control, not whether a father has guaranteed his children's salvation.

verseByVerse.quote: This is why I left you in Crete, so that you might put what remained into order, and appoint elders in every town as I directed you— if anyone is above reproach, the husband of one wife, and his children are believers and not open to the charge of debauchery or insubordination.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is why I left you in Crete, so that you might put what remained into order, and appoint elders in every town as I directed you— if anyone is above reproach, the husband of one wife, and his children are believers and not open to the charge of debauchery or insubordination.

This is why I left you in Crete. Not abandoned: the verb describes a deliberate posting. Crete is a large island south of Greece. Acts records Paul only passing along its coast as a prisoner (Acts 27:7–13); the work there likely came after his release from his first imprisonment. Homer called it Crete of the hundred cities; Paul and Titus had planted churches in several but had not finished organising them.

So that you might put what remained into order. “Put into order” (epidiorthōsē) means to set right further, to straighten out what remains. Its root was used by doctors for setting a broken bone and by craftsmen for straightening what was bent. What remained concedes that the work was unfinished: the churches on Crete were real but not yet in working order, and the chief need was proper leadership.

And appoint elders in every town. “Appoint” (katastēsēs) means to set in place, put in charge. “Elders” (presbyteroi) is plural: each town’s church was to have several elders. Each local church across the island needed its own leadership (Acts 14:23). Paul’s answer to disorder is not a stronger central figure but properly constituted local leadership, which is why Titus’s job seems meant to work himself out of a job. Churches still differ over how this pattern is carried on: Presbyterian churches join elders of many congregations in wider courts, Baptist and Congregational churches keep each church self-governing under its own elders, and Anglican and other episcopal churches see in Titus himself an early form of the bishop who oversees many congregations. All agree that every church needs qualified, godly leaders.

As I directed you. “Directed” (dietaxamēn) means arranged, gave orders. Paul had already given instructions verbally; he now puts them in writing for Titus’s authority, so that nobody on Crete could say Titus was acting on his own.

In the flow. The whole letter turns on verse 5. Paul has just said where the truth comes from (vv. 1–4); now he says what Titus is to do with it, and the rest of the letter unpacks this one sentence. The right men must be put in place (vv. 6–9), because the wrong men are already talking (vv. 10–16). Once the leaders are sound, the households of chapter 2 and the citizens of chapter 3 can be taught to live in a way that fits sound doctrine.

If anyone is above reproach. “Above reproach” (anenklētos) means unaccused, blameless, nothing outstanding that anyone can lay hold of, as with deacons in 1 Timothy 3:10. It is the headline qualification, repeated in verse 7, and the qualifications run closely parallel to 1 Timothy 3.

The husband of one wife. Literally a one-woman man: faithful in marriage, devoted to one woman (1 Timothy 3:2). The phrase speaks of faithfulness rather than issuing a ruling on every question of remarriage. Some read it as forbidding polygamy, others as forbidding any remarriage after divorce, others as requiring that elders be married. The more likely reading is that Paul asks for a man faithful to his wife. A single man is not excluded, since Paul himself was single. A man divorced long ago, or as the innocent party, may qualify if his life is now above reproach, and the church must judge each case with care. And the qualification assumes that elders are men, as in 1 Timothy 2:12 and 3:2: the office of elder belongs to qualified men. This commentary holds that view (often called complementarian) because Paul grounds it in creation rather than local custom (1 Timothy 2:13). Many faithful Christians read these passages differently, and the point is never that women are less gifted or less valued: Paul’s letters are full of women in gospel work (Romans 16:1–7).

And his children are believers. “Believers” (pista) can mean either believing or faithful, in the sense of trustworthy, well-behaved. Some think it requires that an elder’s children all be professing Christians; others that they be faithful, well-ordered and respectful. In 1 Timothy an overseer must keep his children submissive (1 Timothy 3:4); here the following phrase, not open to the charge of debauchery or insubordination, suggests the emphasis is on their behaviour: children who are under his authority and are not wild or rebellious. This concerns children still at home.

And not open to the charge of debauchery or insubordination. “Debauchery” (asōtia) is wild, reckless living, dissipation; a closely related word describes the prodigal son’s reckless living (Luke 15:13). “Insubordination” (anypotaktos) means rebellious, unruly. If an elder cannot lead his own household, he cannot lead the church (1 Timothy 3:5). On a new mission field with a first generation of converts, the practical sense is plain: a man whose own household is visibly out of control is not the man to set a town’s church in order.

A flock bought with blood. Why does it matter so much who leads a house church in a Cretan town? Paul told the Ephesian elders that the Holy Spirit had made them overseers, to care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood (Acts 20:28). The churches Titus is setting in order belong to Christ, who paid for them with his life, and their elders are under-shepherds answering to the Chief Shepherd (1 Peter 5:4). That is why the qualifications start with the home: a man who will not give himself for his own wife and children cannot be trusted with people for whom Christ gave himself. The husband of one wife is to love her as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25), so that his marriage becomes a small, visible copy of the faithfulness of the true Shepherd.

Where Christians differ: must an elder’s children be converted? Some insist that all an elder’s children must be professing Christians. This commentary’s view: Since conversion is God’s work and not under a father’s control (John 1:13), and the word can mean faithful in the sense of trustworthy, it is better to read this as requiring that his children at home be orderly and respectful, not openly wild or rebellious, showing that he leads his household well. A father who has faithfully raised his children and whose child has not yet professed faith is not thereby disqualified, but a household in open disorder would disqualify him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean an elder must be married or have children; it describes how he must behave if he does. Nor does it require that adult children who have left home live in a certain way; the focus is the household under his authority.

Why does Paul care so much about an elder’s home? Because the home is where a man’s character is seen without a pulpit. Anyone can look godly for an hour on Sunday; his wife and children see him on Monday night. A man who is harsh, absent, or indifferent at home will be the same with the church, and a man who leads his family with patient, self-giving love is showing the very skills a church needs. That is why Paul puts the household first. It is also a reminder for every Christian husband and father, elder or not: your home is your first congregation, and the way you love your wife and children is the truest test of your faith.

If my child has walked away from the faith, have I failed? Not necessarily, and you should not carry a guilt God has not laid on you. No parent can give a child a new heart; that is God’s work (John 1:13). Faithful parents in Scripture had wayward children, and God himself, the perfect Father, had rebellious children in Israel (Isaiah 1:2). Ask honestly whether there are ways you need to repent, and if so, confess them to God and, where it would help, to your child. Then keep praying, keep loving, keep the door open, and keep living the gospel in front of them. The prodigal’s father never stopped watching the road.

In a sentence. Unfinished churches are set in order by the right leaders, and the first place to look for them is the home, where a man’s faithfulness to his wife and his care for his children show what kind of shepherd he would be.

In everyday life. An elder’s home carries the weight of the church as well as its own, and his wife and children feel it most. They are rarely thanked. A meal left on the step, an evening of babysitting or a kind note to the family can be the quiet support that keeps a shepherd’s household strong.

For worship. The churches of Crete were real but unfinished, like a broken bone not yet set, and the Lord of the church did not leave them so. He sent a man with instructions, and he has been setting his people straight ever since: patiently, town by town and home by home, with the skill of a physician who knows exactly where it hurts and the tenderness of one who bled for the patient. Nothing he begins is left half-done. The household he is building out of fathers, wives, children and elders will one day stand complete, and every one of its members will owe his place to the Son who gave himself for it.
verseByVerse.note: Crete is a large island south of Greece. Acts records Paul only touching at it as a prisoner (Acts 27:7–13); this later work there is not in Acts.

verseByVerse.quote: For an overseer, as God's steward, must be above reproach. He must not be arrogant or quick-tempered or a drunkard or violent or greedy for gain, but hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined. He must hold firm to the trustworthy word as taught, so that he may be able to give instruction in sound doctrine and also to rebuke those who contradict it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For an overseer, as God’s steward, must be above reproach. He must not be arrogant or quick-tempered or a drunkard or violent or greedy for gain, but hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined. He must hold firm to the trustworthy word as taught, so that he may be able to give instruction in sound doctrine and also to rebuke those who contradict it.

For an overseer. Paul now switches terms, elder in verse 5 and overseer (episkopos) here. The two words describe the same office, used interchangeably within two verses, in the middle of one sentence about one set of men. This is clear evidence that in the New Testament, elders and overseers (bishops) were the same people, as scholars of most traditions agree; churches with bishops generally see the single bishop as a later development from apostolic delegates like Titus.

As God’s steward, must be above reproach. “Steward” (oikonomos) means household manager. In a large household the steward, very often a trusted slave, ran the estate on the owner’s behalf. The title carries real authority and no ownership whatever: he spends another man’s money and answers for it (1 Timothy 3:15).

A steward in the Son’s house. The steward runs a house that is not his, and Hebrews names its owner. Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant, but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son, and we are his house (Hebrews 3:5–6). The elder is never the master of the congregation; he is a servant managing the household of the Son, spending what the Son bought and answering to him for every soul (Hebrews 13:17). It explains why self-will and greed stand at either end of the list of what he must not be. A self-willed steward behaves as though the house were his; a greedy one helps himself to what belongs to another. Both have forgotten whose house it is.

He must not be arrogant. Then five things he must not be, and they read like a portrait of a bad manager. “Arrogant” (authadēs) means self-willed: stubborn, insisting on his own way, the man who suits himself. A man who must always have his way cannot lead God’s household. Underneath it is usually a hunger for control, the fear of what might happen if he were not in charge. Only a man who no longer needs to run everything, because he trusts the one who does, can be trusted with a church.

Or quick-tempered, or a drunkard or violent. “Quick-tempered” (orgilos) means prone to anger, irritable, the man with a short fuse. Drunkard and violent are as in 1 Timothy 3:3; violent means a striker, a man who hits people, whether with his fists or his words.

Or greedy for gain. “Greedy for gain” (aischrokerdēs) means fond of dishonest profit, as with deacons (1 Timothy 3:8). On Crete this was the live issue: the false teachers were in it for shameful gain (v. 11), and a man who wants money should not be given charge of a church’s.

But hospitable, a lover of good. Then six he must be. “Hospitable” (philoxenos) is literally a lover of strangers, and in a world without inns worth staying in, the church ran on it: travelling preachers, refugees, the poor, all needed a believer’s home. “Lover of good” (philagathos) means loving goodness, good people and good things, the opposite of those who in the last days will not love good (2 Timothy 3:3).

Self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined. “Self-controlled” (sōphrōn) means sensible, of sound mind. “Upright” (dikaios) means righteous, just in his dealings with people. “Holy” (hosios) means devout toward God. “Disciplined” (enkratēs) means self-mastered, in control of his desires: a man with a grip on himself.

Character first. Every item so far is about character, and only then does verse 9 give the single competence. The one skill demanded is inseparable from the man exercising it. On an island of empty talkers (v. 10), the difference between a true elder and a false teacher was never going to be fluency.

He must hold firm to the trustworthy word as taught. “Hold firm” (antechomai) means to cling to, to hold on against opposition. “Trustworthy word” (pistos logos) is the reliable message. “As taught” (kata tēn didachēn) means in accordance with the teaching: the apostolic doctrine as it was handed to him, rather than as he has developed it. An elder must be firmly committed to it, not wavering.

So that he may be able to give instruction in sound doctrine. “Give instruction” (parakalein) means to exhort, encourage. “Sound” (hygiainousa) means healthy, the word from which we get hygiene. Sound doctrine makes people spiritually well. This is his positive task: feeding the flock.

And also to rebuke those who contradict it. “Rebuke” (elenchein) means to refute, expose, convict. “Contradict” (antilegontas) means to speak against. This is his negative task: protecting the flock from wolves. Both are necessary, and the two halves must be kept together. A man who can only encourage will watch the flock be eaten; a man who can only refute will do the eating himself. Paul requires both.

What it does not mean. It does not mean elders must be perfect. They are sinners saved by grace. It means their lives show mature, consistent godliness, and their doctrine is sound.

How should a church choose its elders? By looking for these qualities over time, not by electing the most successful, wealthy or outspoken men. Watch how a man treats his family, handles money, responds to criticism and serves when no one is looking. Ask whether he knows and loves the Bible and can explain it to others, and whether he can gently but firmly answer error. Give him time to be tested (1 Timothy 3:10; 5:22). Pray, as the church in Antioch did, before laying hands on anyone. Churches differ on who makes the final choice, the congregation, the existing elders or a wider body, but the qualities to look for are the same in all of them. And remember that the qualities are the same ones God wants in every believer; elders are simply men in whom they are mature enough to be an example.

What if my elders fall short of this list? Every elder falls short in some measure, and you should pray for them and bear with their weaknesses as they bear with yours. If a fault is minor, speak to them privately and kindly, or simply cover it with love (1 Peter 4:8). If it is serious and persistent, a pattern of anger, drunkenness, greed, harshness or false teaching, it should be raised with the other elders, with evidence, following 1 Timothy 5:19–20. An elder who is clearly disqualified should step down, and a church does him and itself no kindness by pretending otherwise. Never use the list as a weapon; use it as a standard everyone is glad to be held to.

In a sentence. An elder manages a household that belongs to God, so he must be a man of tested character, free of self-will, temper and greed, and gripped by the apostles’ teaching, so that he can both feed the flock and guard it.

In everyday life. Almost every item on this list is meant for every Christian; elders are simply men in whom the Spirit’s fruit has ripened. Hospitality is the most practical of them and the easiest to postpone, yet Christ welcomed us when we were strangers (Romans 15:7). An open door and an extra plate at the table were how the early church grew, and they still are.

For worship. One man has borne every quality in this list without a flaw. He was never self-willed, for he came not to do his own will. He was never quick-tempered, but slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love. He was never violent or greedy, but gave himself and his blood for his church. He welcomed strangers, loved what is good, was upright before men and holy before God, and held the Father’s word so firmly that he answered the devil with it. He feeds his flock with healthy teaching and drives off the wolves, and he will not lose one of his sheep.
verseByVerse.note: “Elder” (v. 5) and “overseer” here describe the same office.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Why the right elders matter: deceivers, many from the circumcision party, are overturning whole households for money. Titus must stop their mouths and rebuke sharply, so that people are made sound.
verseByVerse.theology:
Quoting a Pagan, and Agreeing With Him

Paul endorses Epimenides' verdict on Crete (vv. 12–13) not as a racial claim but as the island's own accurate self-assessment, and he rebukes sharply so that the offenders ‘may be sound in the faith’.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Deceivers overturning whole households must be silenced (v. 11), while the deceived are handled gently (2 Timothy 2:25).

Now: ‘To the pure all things are pure’ (v. 15) abolishes ritual defilement, not sin.

verseByVerse.quote: For there are many who are insubordinate, empty talkers and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision party. They must be silenced, since they are upsetting whole families by teaching for shameful gain what they ought not to teach.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For there are many who are insubordinate, empty talkers and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision party. They must be silenced, since they are upsetting whole families by teaching for shameful gain what they ought not to teach.

For there are many who are insubordinate. The for ties this to the elder qualifications: this is why Titus needs men who can rebuke. And many is not encouraging; the problem on Crete was not a fringe. “Insubordinate” (anypotaktoi) means rebellious, refusing to be under anything: the same word used of an elder’s children in verse 6. They would not submit to apostolic authority.

Empty talkers and deceivers. “Empty talkers” (mataiologoi) are literally vain-speakers, idle talkers, speakers of nonsense, men whose words carry nothing (1 Timothy 1:6). “Deceivers” (phrenapatai) are mind-deceivers, seducers of the mind. The first describes the content, the second the effect: there is nothing in what they say, and it still leads people astray.

Especially those of the circumcision party. “Of the circumcision” (hoi ek tēs peritomēs) means Jewish Christians, or those influenced by them, who insisted on circumcision and the law of Moses, as in Galatia (Galatians 2:12; Acts 15:1, 5). There was a large Jewish community on Crete. Their teaching mixed Jewish myths, purity rules and speculation (v. 14; 3:9). Titus of all people knew what was at stake, having been the test case at Jerusalem (Galatians 2:3).

They must be silenced. Paul is blunt. “Silenced” (epistomizein) means to stop the mouth, to muzzle; the picture is of a muzzle or a bridle. Not by force, but by refuting them with sound doctrine (v. 9) and by refusing them a teaching platform in the church. That sits alongside the gentleness Paul commands elsewhere, correcting opponents with gentleness (2 Timothy 2:25), and the two are not in conflict once you see what he distinguishes. Gentleness governs how you treat the deceived. Silencing is for those doing the deceiving, when a congregation is being destroyed while the discussion continues.

Since they are upsetting whole families. “Upsetting” (anatrepousin) means overturning, as in 2 Timothy 2:18. “Whole families” (holous oikous) means entire households. The object is not individuals but households, which on Crete were the churches, since churches met in homes. False teaching could overturn a household’s faith and thus a whole house church at once.

By teaching for shameful gain what they ought not to teach. “Shameful gain” (aischrou kerdous) means dishonest profit. They taught for money (1 Timothy 6:5). There it is again, as in every one of these letters: money underneath the false teaching. It is the very thing that disqualifies an elder (v. 7), and the contrast is exact: the man who must not be greedy for gain, set against the men who teach for it.

Christ plus nothing. Why was the circumcision party so dangerous that its mouths had to be stopped? Because circumcision demanded as a condition of belonging to God says that Christ is not enough. Paul had told the Galatians that if they accepted circumcision on those terms, Christ would be of no advantage to them (Galatians 5:2–4). A teaching that adds a rite to the cross does not add to the gospel; it replaces it. Titus, the uncircumcised Greek whom the Jerusalem leaders had not compelled to be circumcised, could not treat it as a difference of emphasis while whole families were being taught to trust in something besides Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jewish believers were the problem as such; Paul himself was Jewish. The problem was teaching that added the law to Christ. Nor does silenced mean persecution or civil punishment; it means refutation and exclusion from teaching in the church.

How does a church silence false teachers today? By the means Paul gives, not by force. Elders who know the Bible answer the error clearly and publicly, so that the flock is not confused. False teachers are not given the pulpit, the Bible study, the youth group or the church newsletter. If a member persists in spreading serious error after patient correction, the church may have to remove him (3:10–11). Online, it means not sharing or promoting such teaching, and warning those in your care. None of this involves cruelty, slander or calling on the state to punish anyone. It is a shepherd closing the gate on the wolf.

Is it wrong for a teacher to be paid? No. Paul insists that those who labour in preaching and teaching deserve to be supported (1 Timothy 5:17–18). The sin here is teaching for shameful gain: shaping the message to make money, teaching what pleases the paying audience, or using religion as a business. The signs are not hard to spot: constant appeals for money, promises that giving will make you rich, a lifestyle far above the people who fund it, and no accountability. Support faithful teachers gladly. Be wary of anyone whose message always seems to end with your wallet.

In a sentence. Teaching that adds anything to Christ, especially when it is peddled for money, wrecks whole families, so it must be firmly answered and kept out of the church’s teaching.

In everyday life. The voices that shape a family’s faith now come through phones and speakers as well as through the front door. A household can be quietly overturned by them without anyone noticing. It is worth knowing who is teaching the people under your roof, and gladly supporting the ones who teach Christ faithfully.

For worship. The Good Shepherd does not fleece his sheep. He gave his life for them. The false teachers on Crete came for what they could get; Christ came with nothing to gain and everything to give, and he still guards the households that belong to him. He has appointed shepherds to stop the mouths of wolves, and one day he will stop them all himself, when every empty word is silenced and his voice alone is heard.

verseByVerse.quote: One of the Cretans, a prophet of their own, said, "Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons." This testimony is true. Therefore rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith,
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of the Cretans, a prophet of their own, said, “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons.” This testimony is true. Therefore rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith,

One of the Cretans, a prophet of their own, said. Paul is quoting a pagan. The line is usually traced to Epimenides of Knossos, a Cretan poet-prophet of the sixth century BC, whom the Greeks regarded as a seer. Paul calls him a prophet in the sense the Cretans themselves used, not claiming that he was a true prophet of God. He does the same elsewhere, quoting Greek poets at Athens (Acts 17:28) and to the Corinthians (1 Corinthians 15:33).

Cretans are always liars. The reputation was real and proverbial. The Greeks had a verb, krētizein, to Cretanise, meaning to lie. One reason: Cretans claimed to have the tomb of Zeus, which to other Greeks was the founding Cretan falsehood, since they thought Zeus immortal. The contrast with God who never lies (v. 2) is pointed.

Evil beasts. “Evil beasts” (kaka thēria) means wild, dangerous animals: savage, brutal.

Lazy gluttons. Literally idle bellies (gasteres argai): people driven by their appetites and unwilling to work.

This testimony is true. Then Paul says it flatly. An apostle endorses a pagan poet’s description of his own people, in a letter of Scripture, and it needs care. Paul agrees that it describes the false teachers well: they lie, they are brutal in upsetting families, and they are driven by greed. Two things keep it from being what it looks like. First, Paul is not making a racial claim about Cretans as such. He has just left elders and congregations there, and Titus is to build them up. What he affirms is that the island’s own moral self-assessment was accurate, and that the false teachers he has just described are living down to it. A Cretan said this about Crete; Paul agrees that the cap fits the men in question.

Therefore rebuke them sharply. Second, note the purpose clause, because it changes everything. “Rebuke” (elenche) means refute, convict. “Sharply” (apotomōs) means severely, cuttingly, abruptly; its root is the verb to cut off. The situation called for decisive correction, not gentle persuasion alone. Sharpness aimed at someone’s soundness is not cruelty. Contrast 2 Timothy 2:25, where gentleness is urged. The pastoral judgment underneath is that different people need different treatment. Timothy, perhaps more naturally timid, was told to be gentle and patient. Titus, on Crete, is told to cut. Paul has no single register, and a minister who only ever has one has not learned from him.

That they may be sound in the faith. “Sound” (hygiainōsin) means healthy. The sharpness has an aim, and the aim is their health. Sound is the medical word: Paul wants these people well. The goal of the sharp rebuke is restoration, not destruction. Them probably refers to the church members who were being influenced, and perhaps the false teachers themselves. A rebuke intended to make somebody healthy is a different act from a rebuke intended to put them in their place, even when the words are identical.

Sound in the faith of the truthful one. What makes a liar healthy? Not a sharper rebuke on its own. The rebuke clears the way; the cure is the faith it calls people back to, and that faith rests on a person. Jesus said, I am the way, and the truth, and the life (John 14:6), and he came, he said, not for the healthy but for the sick (Mark 2:17). The Cretan proverb was a diagnosis, and Paul does not dispute it. But the same letter will announce that the grace of God has appeared, training people to renounce ungodliness (2:11–12). Christ, the faithful and true witness (Revelation 3:14), is the health that Titus’s sharp words were meant to bring them back to.

What it does not mean. It does not license ethnic stereotyping of people today. Paul is quoting a Cretan’s self-criticism to describe the false teachers’ character, and Paul’s own aim is that Cretans become sound in the faith; the gospel transforms every people. Nor does quoting a pagan poet mean his words are inspired; Paul’s use of them is inspired, as a true observation.

Is the saying self-refuting, since a Cretan said all Cretans are liars? Logicians have enjoyed the puzzle for centuries, but it is not what Paul is doing. It is a proverb about a people’s character, not a logical claim about every single Cretan on every occasion, and Paul agrees only with the observation it makes. Quoting a pagan writer’s true statement does not make him an inspired prophet, any more than quoting a newspaper makes it Scripture. All truth is God’s truth, and Paul is free to use it wherever he finds it.

How do I know when to rebuke sharply and when gently? Look at the person and the danger. Gentleness is right for the confused, the weak, the young believer who has stumbled, and anyone willing to listen (Galatians 6:1; 2 Timothy 2:24–25). Sharpness is right when someone is knowingly leading others astray, when gentle words have been ignored, or when great harm is being done and must be stopped at once. Even then, the aim must be the person’s health, never your own satisfaction. Check your motive: would you be glad if they repented and you never got the credit? Most of us lean naturally to one register; ask God to give you the other when it is needed.

In a sentence. Paul agrees with Crete’s own poet that the false teachers fit the island’s old reputation, and he orders sharp words for them, but only so that they may be made well in the faith.

In everyday life. The grace that reached Crete does not leave a people as it finds them. Name one sin your culture or family is known for, one you are tempted to excuse because everyone shares it, and ask God this week to make you different there.

For worship. The gospel came to an island of liars, beasts and idle bellies and planted churches in it. That is the glory of God’s grace: he does not wait for a better people. He sent his Son to the Cretans, and to us, and makes liars into truthful men, savages into gentle ones, and the lazy into those zealous for good works. The God who cannot lie has spoken his word to a lying world, and it is changing the world one household at a time.
verseByVerse.note: The line is usually traced to Epimenides, a Cretan poet-prophet of about 600 BC.

verseByVerse.quote: not devoting themselves to Jewish myths and the commands of people who turn away from the truth. To the pure, all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure; but both their minds and their consciences are defiled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
not devoting themselves to Jewish myths and the commands of people who turn away from the truth. To the pure, all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure; but both their minds and their consciences are defiled.

Not devoting themselves to Jewish myths. “Devoting themselves” (prosechontes) means paying attention to, as in 1 Timothy 1:4. “Jewish myths” (Ioudaikoi mythoi) are speculative stories and legends drawn from Jewish tradition, not Scripture itself. It is the same material as at Ephesus, myths and endless genealogies.

And the commands of people who turn away from the truth. “Commands of people” (entolai anthrōpōn) are human rules. Jesus condemned the same thing (Mark 7:7–8, quoting Isaiah 29:13). These were probably purity rules about food and ritual washing, as the next verse suggests (Colossians 2:20–23). Speculation on one side and man-made commands on the other: fantasy and legalism, which look like opposites and regularly arrive together. Why together? Because both offer something grace does not: secret knowledge to feel superior with, and rules a person can keep and measure himself by. Each lets a religious man feel he stands before God on his own achievement, and the gospel takes that away from both.

To the pure, all things are pure. Then verse 15, which is easily misused. The first half is a genuine principle: purity (kathara, clean) is a matter of the heart, not of external rules. Against teachers imposing food laws and ritual restrictions, he says that for a person made clean by God, created things are clean. For those whose hearts have been cleansed by faith (Acts 15:9), no food or created thing is defiling in itself (Mark 7:15, 19; Romans 14:14, 20). It is the same argument as 1 Timothy 4:4, that everything created by God is good.

But to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure. The second half is the sharper observation. “Defiled” (memiammenois) means stained, polluted. “Unbelieving” (apistois) means without faith, not trusting God. Defilement is not in the object but in the eye. A corrupted mind manages to corrupt whatever it handles, including good and innocent things, and such a man cannot be cleaned by rules about food, because the trouble is not in the food.

But both their minds and their consciences are defiled. “Minds” (nous) means thinking, reasoning. “Consciences” (syneidēsis) means moral awareness. Two faculties, and between them a man is finished. The mind judges what is true; the conscience judges what is right. When both are stained, there is no internal instrument left to detect the problem (1 Timothy 4:2), which is precisely why such men are confident, and why they must be silenced rather than reasoned with. The problem is not what they eat, but who they are.

Who makes the pure pure. Paul’s principle raises the question of where pure people come from, since by nature every mind and conscience is in the condition of the second half of the verse. The answer is Christ, twice over. He is the one who, Mark tells us, declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19; the KJV renders the phrase differently, but most modern Bibles take it as Mark’s comment), so that the food rules the Cretan teachers were pressing had already been set aside by the Lord himself. And he is the one whose blood cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7). The pure of verse 15 are not people who have kept the rules better, but defiled people whom Christ has washed, and to them he hands back the whole created world as clean.

What it does not mean. To the pure, all things are pure does not mean that nothing is sinful for a believer, or that a pure person can do anything. Paul is speaking of created things like food, not of sin. Sin remains sin. Nor does it mean a believer should ignore a weaker brother’s conscience (Romans 14:13–21). The verse abolishes ritual defilement; it does not abolish sin.

Does this mean I can watch or enjoy anything if my heart is pure? No. The verse is about created things that are good in themselves, food, drink, days, the material world, not about things that are sinful in their nature or that feed sin in us. Pornography, cruelty and blasphemy are not made clean by a believer watching them; and a pure heart is exactly the heart that does not want to be stained by them (Philippians 4:8). A Christian is free to enjoy God’s good gifts with thanksgiving. He is not free to call evil good. If you find yourself using this verse to justify something your conscience is uneasy about, that unease is worth listening to.

How do I get a clean conscience? Not by keeping more rules, but by the blood of Christ. Hebrews says the blood of Christ purifies our conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Hebrews 9:14). Bring your guilt to him by name and confess it; he is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse (1 John 1:9). Then believe what he says: you are clean. A conscience that keeps accusing you of forgiven sin needs to be taught by Scripture to rest in Christ’s finished work. And keep it clean by walking in the light, dealing with sin quickly instead of letting it build up. A conscience is a gift; treat it gently and keep it tender.

In a sentence. Defilement lives in the heart, not in food or rules, so no rule can clean a stained mind, but a heart washed by Christ can receive all God’s good gifts as clean.

In everyday life. Enjoy one of God’s good gifts today, a meal, a walk, a conversation, with conscious thanks, and refuse one thing you know would stain your mind.

For worship. Under the old law, touching the unclean made a man unclean. Then the Holy One came, and the current ran the other way. He laid his hand on a leper, and the leper was clean; a woman who had bled for twelve years touched his garment and was made well; he ate with sinners, and they went home forgiven. Nothing defiled could defile him, and whatever he touched in mercy he made pure. At the last he went outside the camp and bore our uncleanness himself, so that people with stained minds and consciences could be given clean hearts, and a clean world to give thanks in.

verseByVerse.quote: They profess to know God, but they deny him by their works. They are detestable, disobedient, unfit for any good work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They profess to know God, but they deny him by their works. They are detestable, disobedient, unfit for any good work.

They profess to know God. It is the sentence the whole chapter has been building toward. These men are not atheists and would be insulted to be called unbelievers. “Profess” (homologousin) means to confess, to claim openly. They make the claim, publicly and probably loudly, perhaps claiming special knowledge of God through their myths and rules.

But they deny him by their works. “Deny” (arnountai) means to disown, renounce. The two verbs are set against each other deliberately. Confession and denial are the great pair in the New Testament: whoever confesses me before men, and whoever denies me (Matthew 10:32–33). Paul says a man can perform the first with his mouth while performing the second with his life, and that the second is the one that counts. Their lives contradict their claims (2 Timothy 3:5; 1 John 2:4). The test of knowing God is obedience (James 2:14–26).

Lord, Lord. The sharpest commentary on this verse came from Jesus himself. Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, will enter the kingdom of heaven, he said, but the one who does the will of my Father; and to some who had prophesied and done mighty works in his name he will say, I never knew you (Matthew 7:21–23). The Cretan teachers claimed to know God. The question at the last will be whether God, in Christ, knows them. For anyone frightened by this hard verse, that is the comfort: knowing God is not finally a claim we make but a relationship he creates, and those whom the Son makes his own he also makes fit for good works (2:14).

A hard case for any church. This is the same figure as 2 Timothy 3:5, having the appearance of godliness but denying its power. An open opponent can be answered; a man whose profession is orthodox and whose life contradicts it cannot be, and he is usually inside.

They are detestable. Three words follow, and they escalate. “Detestable” (bdelyktoi) means abominable, disgusting. The word is related to the Old Testament term for an abomination to God, used in the Greek Old Testament of idols and unclean things. Ironically, they were obsessed with avoiding what was impure; yet they themselves were abominable. Men who talk endlessly about purity are pronounced unclean. The second word, “disobedient” (apeitheis), means refusing to be persuaded, rebellious: a different word from the insubordination of verse 10, but the same refusal to be ruled.

Unfit for any good work. “Unfit” (adokimoi) is the assayer’s term for metal tested and rejected: failing the test, disqualified, worthless, as in 2 Timothy 3:8. It closes the chapter on the note that opened it, a knowledge of the truth which accords with godliness (v. 1). And good work (ergon agathon) introduces a theme of the whole letter: believers must be devoted to good works (2:7, 14; 3:1, 8, 14). The phrase comes again and again in three short chapters, and it starts here, with men who are fit for none. It also sets up what comes next: But as for you (2:1). Against men fit for no good work, Titus is to teach a church whose ordinary lives fit sound doctrine.

What it does not mean. It does not mean good works save. Paul teaches clearly that we are saved not by works but by mercy (3:5). But true saving faith always produces good works (Ephesians 2:10). A profession of faith with no good works is empty. Paul is not about to argue that works save; he will say the opposite as plainly as it can be said. He is going to argue that grace produces them, and that a profession which produces none has already been tested and failed.

If I still sin a lot, am I denying God by my works? The fact that this question troubles you is a good sign. Paul is describing people whose lives as a whole contradict their profession, who are comfortable in disobedience and unfit for any good work, not believers who fight sin and often lose. Every Christian still sins (1 John 1:8), and the difference is not perfection but direction: do you hate your sin, confess it, and keep returning to Christ? Are there good works in your life, however small, that come from love for him? Then you are not the man in this verse. Keep looking to Christ, whose righteousness covers you, and whose Spirit is changing you.

What good works does God want from ordinary Christians? Mostly ordinary ones, done for his sake. Titus 2 and 3 will fill them in: loving your spouse and children, working honestly, being self-controlled, submitting to rightful authorities, being kind and gentle to everyone, helping those in urgent need, speaking evil of no one. Good works are not only religious activities; they are the whole of life lived in obedience and love. Ephesians 2:10 says God prepared them beforehand for us to walk in, so look for them in the place he has put you: your home, your street, your workplace, your church.

In a sentence. Knowing God is shown by the life, not the claim, and a profession that produces no good works has already been tested and found false.

In everyday life. The gap between Sunday’s words and Tuesday’s deeds is where this verse bites, and most of us know where our own gap is. Closing it is rarely dramatic, and it is the fruit of Christ’s Spirit in you, not a price for his acceptance: a debt paid, an apology made, a neighbour helped. These are the works by which hands begin to say what the mouth says on Sunday.

For worship. One man’s works and words never once contradicted each other. Christ professed to know the Father and proved it in every deed, and could ask his enemies which of them convicted him of sin. Put to every test, in the wilderness, in Gethsemane, before Pilate and on the cross, he came out pure gold. Then he did the greatest good work of all and gave himself for people who had failed every test, and now he sits as a refiner over the worthless metal of human lives and does not stop until it shines. The hollow men of Crete are answered by a Saviour approved in everything, who makes the disqualified fit for every good work.

1.text: <sup>1</sup>Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ, for the sake of the faith of God's elect and their knowledge of the truth, which accords with godliness,<sup>2</sup>in hope of eternal life, which God, who never lies, promised before the ages began<sup>3</sup>and at the proper time manifested in his word through the preaching with which I have been entrusted by the command of God our Savior;<sup>4</sup>To Titus, my true child in a common faith: Grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior.<sup>5</sup>This is why I left you in Crete, so that you might put what remained into order, and appoint elders in every town as I directed you—<sup>6</sup>if anyone is above reproach, the husband of one wife, and his children are believers and not open to the charge of debauchery or insubordination.<sup>7</sup>For an overseer, as God's steward, must be above reproach. He must not be arrogant or quick-tempered or a drunkard or violent or greedy for gain,<sup>8</sup>but hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined.<sup>9</sup>He must hold firm to the trustworthy word as taught, so that he may be able to give instruction in sound doctrine and also to rebuke those who contradict it.<sup>10</sup>For there are many who are insubordinate, empty talkers and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision party.<sup>11</sup>They must be silenced, since they are upsetting whole families by teaching for shameful gain what they ought not to teach.<sup>12</sup>One of the Cretans, a prophet of their own, said, "Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons."<sup>13</sup>This testimony is true. Therefore rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith,<sup>14</sup>not devoting themselves to Jewish myths and the commands of people who turn away from the truth.<sup>15</sup>To the pure, all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure; but both their minds and their consciences are defiled.<sup>16</sup>They profess to know God, but they deny him by their works. They are detestable, disobedient, unfit for any good work.

2.title: Adorning the Doctrine: The Gospel-Shaped Community
2.overview:
Paul tells Titus how each group in the church should live: older men, older women, younger women, younger men, Titus himself, and slaves. Each instruction carries a missionary reason: so that God’s word is not slandered (v. 5), so that opponents have nothing bad to say (v. 8), so that slaves “adorn the doctrine of God our Savior” (v. 10).

Then the reason underneath it all (vv. 11–14). The grace of God has appeared in Christ, and that same grace trains us to say no to ungodliness and to live well now, while we wait for the appearing of “our great God and Savior Jesus Christ”, who gave himself to redeem a people eager to do good. Grace saves, and grace trains.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — What Accords With Sound Doctrine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul goes through the church group by group, and each instruction carries a reason: that the watching world may find the gospel credible, and even beautiful.
verseByVerse.theology:
Doctrine Has a Shape

Titus is to teach what accords with sound doctrine (v. 1), its natural clothing, and the climax is slaves adorning the doctrine of God our Saviour (v. 10).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The only reason given for the household instructions is missionary: ‘that the word of God may not be reviled’ (v. 5).

Now: Older women are commanded to teach (vv. 3–4); the close training of young wives is theirs, not Titus’s.

verseByVerse.quote: But as for you, teach what accords with sound doctrine. Older men are to be sober-minded, dignified, self-controlled, sound in faith, in love, and in steadfastness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Titus 2 shows what sound doctrine looks like lived out in a church, and why. Against false teachers whose lives denied God (1:16), Titus must teach what fits healthy doctrine (v. 1), group by group: older men, older women, younger women, younger men with Titus as their model, and slaves, whose honesty makes the doctrine of God attractive (vv. 2–10). Then comes the foundation (vv. 11–14): the grace of God has appeared, training us to live godly lives while we wait for the appearing of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ. The whole chapter moves between two appearings of Christ, and every ordinary duty in it is lit by both.

But as for you, teach what accords with sound doctrine. The contrast is with the empty talkers just described as unfit for any good work (1:10–16). “Accords with” means is fitting, suitable. Titus is not told only to teach sound doctrine, which he must obviously do, but to teach what fits it. The whole chapter is about behaviour, and Paul introduces it as the natural clothing of a body of truth.

Doctrine has a shape. A life either fits doctrine or does not. That is why no theology is expounded for ten verses, only conduct; and when the theology comes in verses 11–14, it turns out to be the reason for every line.

Older men are to be sober-minded. Paul begins with the group most likely to think itself exempt: not the office of elder but the older men of the congregation. “Sober-minded” means temperate, clear-headed, as in 1 Timothy 3:2. Age can bring temptations to excess, complacency or bitterness; older men must stay alert.

Dignified, self-controlled. Serious, worthy of respect; and sensible, sound-minded. Self-control is a keyword of this chapter (vv. 2, 4, 5, 6, 12).

Sound in faith, in love, and in steadfastness. “Sound” is the medical word, and here it attaches not to doctrine but to graces: healthy faith, healthy love, healthy endurance. The familiar triad (1 Corinthians 13:13), with steadfastness in place of hope, since endurance is hope under pressure; and it belongs particularly to age, which is uniquely placed to have learned it and uniquely tempted to abandon it at the end.

Consider him who endured. Where does an old man find steadfastness for the last mile? Hebrews answers: consider him who endured such hostility from sinners, so that you do not grow weary or fainthearted (Hebrews 12:3). Christian endurance is not stoic grit but the patience of people fixed on a Saviour who finished his course. The older man who stays healthy in faith, love and steadfastness is not proving his own staying power; he is being kept by the one who, having loved his own, loved them to the end (John 13:1).

What are the particular dangers of growing old as a Christian? Scripture and experience suggest a few. Cynicism: having seen churches split and leaders fall, it is easy to stop expecting God to do anything. Coldness: love can shrink to a small circle of the familiar. Bitterness over losses and disappointments. Complacency: thinking the battle with sin is over. Self-indulgence, when duties are fewer. And weariness, the temptation to stop serving and let the young get on with it. Paul’s three words answer them: healthy faith that still trusts, healthy love that still reaches out, healthy endurance that keeps going. Moses was eighty when God called him, and Caleb at eighty-five asked for a mountain.

In everyday life. Retirement can feel like being moved to the edge of things, in church as well as at work. Paul thinks otherwise: an older man who is still trusting, still loving and still going is one of the most persuasive sermons a congregation ever hears.

verseByVerse.quote: Older women likewise are to be reverent in behavior, not slanderers or slaves to much wine. They are to teach what is good,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Older women likewise are to be reverent. “Reverent” is a temple word, meaning fitting for a temple, holy in demeanour, as one carries oneself in a sacred place. An older Christian woman should move through ordinary life as though it were holy ground.

Not slanderers. The word is diaboloi, accusers, malicious gossips, the same term used of the devil himself (1 Timothy 3:11). A tongue that circulates accusations is doing the devil’s own work. The pull is often the pleasure of being in the know, which feels like importance. But knowing other people’s troubles is a trust to carry to God, not a currency to spend.

Or slaves to much wine. Enslaved, in settled bondage. The candour is pastoral: congregations that cannot name such things cannot help anyone caught in them. These two are the characteristic temptations of people with time on their hands and less to occupy them than they once had.

They are to teach what is good. One word in Greek, teachers of good, found nowhere else in the Bible, and it is the answer to the two vices: Paul assigns her a job. Older women have a vital teaching ministry: not the public teaching office of elders (1 Timothy 2:12), but a powerful informal ministry, especially to younger women (v. 4), by word and example. Whatever 1 Timothy 2:12 means, it cannot mean women do not teach, because the man who wrote it commands them to.

The accuser and the advocate. The word for gossip is the devil’s own name, set against Christ’s. Satan is the accuser of our brothers, who accuses them day and night before our God (Revelation 12:10); but if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous (1 John 2:1). The accuser tells our faults; the advocate covers them with his own blood. In every conversation she chooses which of the two she will sound like, and one who has been defended by Christ has every reason to defend others.

What it does not mean. It does not limit older women’s teaching to these topics or these hearers; they rightly teach children (2 Timothy 1:5) and may explain the faith in many settings (Acts 18:26).

Does this mean Christians must not drink alcohol? No. The sin is being enslaved to wine, not using it. Scripture calls wine God’s gift to gladden the heart (Psalm 104:15), Jesus made it at a wedding (John 2:1–11), and Paul advised Timothy to take a little (1 Timothy 5:23). But Scripture also warns plainly against drunkenness (Ephesians 5:18), and some, for their own good or for the sake of others, will wisely choose not to drink at all. If you find that you need a drink, that you hide how much you take, or that others are worried, it may already have a hold on you. Tell someone, and get help; there is no shame in seeking freedom.

How can I tell the difference between sharing a concern and gossip? Ask who you are telling and why. Sharing is right when the person you tell can help, or needs to know for someone’s protection, and when you would be content for the person concerned to hear what you said. Gossip passes on another’s faults or troubles to people who cannot help, for the interest of the story, or to make yourself look better. A good test: have I spoken to the person first (Matthew 18:15)? Am I saying this in a way I would be willing to say it to their face? Would I want this said about me? When in doubt, pray about it instead of talking about it.

In everyday life. Many young mothers in a church are quietly overwhelmed, and few say so. An older woman who asks how she is really doing, and stays for the answer, may be the teacher of good Paul has in mind.

verseByVerse.quote: and so train the young women to love their husbands and children, to be self-controlled, pure, working at home, kind, and submissive to their own husbands, that the word of God may not be reviled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And so train the young women. This passage gives modern readers most trouble, so it repays reading exactly. “Train” means to teach to be sensible, from the same root as self-controlled. The older women teach the younger, not Titus: Paul hands the close training of young wives to women who know the road.

To love their husbands and children. Two more single Greek words, husband-loving and child-loving, using the word for warm, affectionate love. These are taught: Paul does not assume affection arrives automatically with marriage and motherhood, or that a woman struggling there is defective. Under the strains of daily life such love can and must be learned, from someone further along, and from the Spirit through whom God’s love has been poured into our hearts (Romans 5:5).

To be self-controlled, pure. Sensible, and chaste, morally clean, sexually faithful.

Working at home. Home-workers, busy at home; some manuscripts read keepers of the home. It means managing the household diligently (1 Timothy 5:14; Proverbs 31:10–31), in contrast with the idle, gossiping younger widows of 1 Timothy 5:13. The first-century household was a productive economic unit, and a competent wife ran a small business. Then kind, good and generous: in a busy household with servants, children and guests, kindness is the quality that makes the home a refuge rather than a workplace.

And submissive to their own husbands. Ordering themselves under, voluntarily yielding: the wife’s respectful following of her husband’s loving leadership (Ephesians 5:22–33; Colossians 3:18; 1 Peter 3:1–6). And the qualifier matters and is regularly dropped: their own husbands. Paul is not describing women as a class under men as a class; he is speaking of a marriage. And it stands within a New Testament frame that tells husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25), a demand which, if anything, costs more.

That the word of God may not be reviled. Then the reason, and it is the only one given here. If Christian wives abandoned their families or flouted their husbands, outsiders would blame the gospel.

A marriage that preaches. Why should the way a young wife runs her home affect what pagans think of the word of God? Because marriage was made to picture Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:32). A Christian home is a small sermon on the gospel, preached without words. When it is cold, chaotic or cruel, the sermon slanders its subject. When husband and wife love each other in that pattern, the watching town is shown, in miniature, the love of the Bridegroom for his bride.

Where Christians differ: does this teach a fixed role for wives in every culture? Egalitarians (who hold that Scripture assigns no distinct roles to husband and wife) argue that Paul is accommodating to first-century culture to avoid offence, and that in a different culture, mutual submission without distinct roles would better adorn the gospel. This commentary’s view: The motive is indeed partly missional (vv. 5, 8, 10). But elsewhere Paul grounds the wife’s submission in Christ’s relationship with the church (Ephesians 5:22–33) and in creation (1 Corinthians 11:8–9), which do not change with culture. This is the complementarian view: husbands and wives are equal in dignity and worth, with distinct and complementary roles. The husband leads with self-sacrificing love like Christ; the wife follows with respect and strength. This never means a wife must obey a command to sin (Acts 5:29), endure abuse, or lose her voice and gifts. Egalitarian Christians reach their view out of the same wish to honour Scripture and adorn the gospel, and this commentary counts them brothers and sisters.

What it does not mean. It does not forbid women from working outside the home; the excellent wife of Proverbs 31 trades, buys land and sells goods. It means the home is not neglected. Nor does it make submission a matter of inferiority; in the work of salvation Christ submitted to the Father, yet is equal with him (1 Corinthians 15:28). And it does not apply to single women, whose calling is equally honourable.

Must a wife submit to an abusive husband? No. Submission is given to a husband in his proper role, as to the Lord; it never means joining in sin, or enduring violence, threats or control. A husband who abuses his wife has abandoned the very headship he claims, which Scripture defines as giving himself up for her.
