A wife in danger should seek safety and help at once, and the church and the law should protect her (Romans 13:4). Leaders must never send her back into harm in the name of submission or reconciliation. Abuse may also be a form of desertion of the marriage covenant, and wise pastors will help her think through what Scripture allows. Persistent, serious abuse can amount to the desertion that Scripture accepts as a ground for divorce (1 Corinthians 7:15; the Westminster Confession 24.5–6), and the elders should help judge her case with her; abuse is never to be tolerated. The church’s first duty is to the vulnerable.

What does submission look like in an ordinary Christian marriage? It looks like a wife who respects her husband, supports his leadership, speaks well of him, and is willing to follow his lead when, after honest discussion, they cannot agree on a decision. It does not mean she has no opinions, never disagrees, or does all the work; a wise husband seeks and values her counsel, as any good leader does. And it is matched by a husband who leads by serving: who takes responsibility, prays with his family, puts his wife’s good before his own, listens, and never uses his headship to get his own way. When both are walking with Christ, submission rarely feels like a burden; it feels like partnership with an order to it.

For worship. The Son of God grew up in an ordinary home and was subject to his parents, and from the cross, in agony, he provided for his mother (Luke 2:51; John 19:26–27). No household duty is beneath the Lord who honoured one. And every home ordered in love points beyond itself to the wedding all the others were made to foreshadow, when the Lamb’s bride sits down at his supper. Married or single, every believer has a place at that table.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, urge the younger men to be self-controlled. Show yourself in all respects to be a model of good works, and in your teaching show integrity, dignity, and sound speech that cannot be condemned, so that an opponent may be put to shame, having nothing evil to say about us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Likewise, urge the younger men to be self-controlled. One instruction, the same word given to older men and younger women (vv. 2, 5), and it covers everything: young men are prone to impulsiveness, anger, lust, pride and recklessness. Sound judgment and self-mastery are what they most need (2 Timothy 2:22).

A model of good works. Then Titus himself. “Model” (typos) is a die, a stamp: Titus is not merely to teach the chapter; he is to be the mould it is struck from.

And in your teaching show integrity. Incorruption, freedom from corrupt motives: teaching with no self-interest mixed in. On an island of men teaching for shameful gain (1:11), that was the visible difference. With it goes dignity, treating the things of God with the seriousness they deserve.

Sound speech that cannot be condemned. A healthy word, beyond criticism. That does not mean speech nobody dislikes; it means speech that gives no legitimate handle.

So that an opponent may be put to shame. Paul assumes there will be opponents, false teachers or unbelieving critics; he aims not at being liked but at giving them nothing true to work with. There is a great difference between a church that is attacked and a church that has handed its attackers the ammunition, and only the second is a disgrace.

Having nothing evil to say about us. The word is us: what a young minister on Crete does will be laid at the door of the whole enterprise, the apostle included. A blameless life silences critics (1 Peter 2:12, 15).

The speech no one could condemn. Paul’s standard for Titus had already been met once. When the chief priests sought testimony against Jesus to put him to death, they found none; many bore false witness against him, but their testimony did not agree (Mark 14:55–56). Every Christian teacher who aims at sound speech is following the one who left us an example (1 Peter 2:21). The difference is that Titus would sometimes fail and need forgiving. Christ never did, and it is his blameless life, not ours, on which our standing rests.

What does self-control look like for a young man today? It means mastering the appetites before they master you. Guarding your eyes and your screen against pornography, with accountability if you need it (Job 31:1). Controlling your temper, especially online and in traffic. Managing money instead of spending on impulse. Keeping your body under control in relationships with women, treating them as sisters in all purity (1 Timothy 5:2). Getting up in the morning and doing your work. Thinking before you speak. None of it is possible by willpower alone; it is the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:23). But the Spirit works through your choices, so make them, and find an older man who will walk with you.

Do I have to be perfect before I can set an example? No. Titus was not perfect, and neither was Paul. A model of good works is someone whose life, taken as a whole, shows what following Christ looks like, including how to repent when you fail. Often the most helpful example a younger believer sees is an older one confessing a sin, apologising, and starting again. What disqualifies an example is hypocrisy: teaching one thing and living another without shame. So aim at consistency, not perfection. Let your life and your words point the same way, and when they do not, say so and put it right.

For worship. Christ was a young man when he did his work, and he mastered what young men cannot. Hungry in the wilderness, he would not turn stones into bread; offered the kingdoms of the world, he would not bow; mocked on the cross, he would not come down. And he does not leave young men to it: he gives his Spirit, whose fruit is self-control, to young men who cannot master themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: Bondservants are to be submissive to their own masters in everything; they are to be well-pleasing, not argumentative, not pilfering, but showing all good faith, so that in everything they may adorn the doctrine of God our Savior.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bondservants are to be submissive. The last group: slaves. In everything means in all that does not require sin (Acts 5:29).

What Paul does and does not do. Paul is not endorsing the institution. He lists enslavers among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10), tells masters they answer to a Master in heaven (Colossians 4:1), most likely tells a slave to take freedom if he can get it (1 Corinthians 7:21), and sends a runaway back as a beloved brother (Philemon 16). What he is doing here is telling people with no legal power how to live with dignity inside a system they cannot change.

They are to be well-pleasing, not argumentative. Well-pleasing is doing their work well. “Argumentative” means talking back, the constant low-level resistance of the powerless; it is the same word used of the false teachers who contradict the truth (1:9).

Not pilfering. Secretly keeping back for oneself, the word used of Ananias keeping back part of the money (Acts 5:2–3). Petty theft was so common that many hardly thought it stealing. Paul does.

But showing all good faith. Complete trustworthiness. Taken together, the picture is a slave whose owner discovers that things stopped going missing and the back-answering stopped, and cannot account for it.

That they may adorn the doctrine. The reason gives the lowliest people in the church a remarkable dignity. “Adorn” (kosmōsin, the root of cosmetic) could be used of arranging jewels so that a stone shows to best advantage. Paul tells slaves, who could be beaten at will, that their honesty in small things displays the doctrine of God to its best advantage. The doctrine is already true; their lives display its beauty.

The setting for the jewel. The doctrine of God our Saviour is, at its centre, the news that the Saviour himself took the form of a servant, a doulos, and became obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:7–8). The gospel was not stooping when it came into the kitchens of Crete; it was coming home to the kind of life the Son of God had chosen. When a man who could pilfer stops pilfering, he looks, in a small way, like the one he trusts, and the most powerless people on the island become the setting in which the jewel is shown.

Why didn’t Paul simply condemn slavery? Because he was writing to a tiny, powerless minority with no means of abolishing it, and his aim in this letter is how believers should live where they are. But he planted the seeds that destroyed it. He taught that slave and master are brothers, equal in Christ (Galatians 3:28; Philemon 16), that masters must treat slaves justly and fairly because they too have a Master (Colossians 4:1), and that slave-trading is a sin against God’s law (1 Timothy 1:10). Where the gospel took hold, Christians in time came to see that the institution itself could not stand alongside it. Slavery as practised in the Atlantic trade, based on kidnapping and race, was condemned by Scripture from the start, since stealing a person to sell him was a capital crime in the law of Moses (Exodus 21:16; 1 Timothy 1:10). To their shame, many professing Christians defended it anyway; others, reading the same Bible, led the fight to end it.

Does this mean I must obey my boss in everything? The principles apply to employees, with differences. You chose your job and can leave it; slaves could not. Within your work, be diligent, respectful, honest and reliable, even with a difficult manager (1 Peter 2:18). Do not talk back, take things home that are not yours, pad your hours or expenses, or quietly do less than you are paid for. But no employer has the right to require sin: falsifying records, deceiving customers, cutting corners on safety, or covering up wrongdoing. There you must obey God rather than men, respectfully, and accept the cost if it comes.

In everyday life. Pilfering rarely feels like theft now either: ten minutes taken here, a padded claim there. Stopping it will probably go unnoticed, but it is exactly the kind of small honesty Paul says makes the doctrine of God beautiful, and in time the people who work beside you will notice.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The reason underneath every household duty: grace has already appeared in Christ, and it trains the people it saves. Christ’s death has made a people of his own, eager to do good, waiting for the glory still to come.
verseByVerse.theology:
Our Great God and Saviour Jesus Christ

By the construction Granville Sharp described, verse 13 names one person, Jesus Christ, our great God and Saviour, closing the letter's alternation of ‘God our Saviour’ and ‘Christ our Saviour’.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Grace appeared to all kinds of people, the slave on the same terms as the master (v. 11).

Now: Grace is the schoolmaster (v. 12), and a people eager for good works is what redemption produces, not its price (v. 14).

verseByVerse.quote: For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the grace of God has appeared. For, and after ten verses of household instruction Paul gives the reason underneath: a summary of the gospel as rich as any he wrote, there to explain why an older woman should not gossip and a slave should not pilfer. “Has appeared” is the shining-out word, used of the sun breaking through (Luke 1:78–79) and of a king making a public appearance. Grace was not merely announced or explained. It showed up, visibly, in a person: in Jesus Christ, in his birth, life, death and resurrection (John 1:14).

An event you could have attended. The tense is past and definite. Paul is not only describing a quality in God’s character; he is describing an event you could have attended, in Bethlehem, in Galilee, outside Jerusalem.

Bringing salvation. Grace does not merely offer salvation; it brings it. It is not a possibility held out but a rescue carried in.

For all people. After old men, old women, young women, young men and slaves (vv. 2–10), all people means all kinds of people: the answer to the graded religion Crete’s teachers offered. The grace of God has appeared to the slave in the kitchen on precisely the same terms as to the master.

Where Christians differ: does grace bring salvation to everyone without exception? Some read this verse as teaching that God’s grace makes salvation available to every individual equally, or even that all will be saved. This commentary’s view: The context shows that all people refers to all kinds and classes of people listed in verses 2–10, as in 1 Timothy 2:4–6. Grace has appeared for every category of humanity, without distinction. And grace that brings salvation actually saves: it trains those it saves (v. 12) and it redeemed a particular people for God’s own possession (v. 14). This is consistent with definite atonement (Christ died to secure the salvation of a particular people) and effectual grace (grace that actually brings a person to faith), while the gospel is still freely offered to everyone. Christians who read the verse more broadly usually share the same eagerness to offer Christ to all.

Grace comes first. Paul does not say: behave well, and then grace may appear. He says behave well because it already has.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all people will be saved; Scripture teaches eternal judgment for those who reject Christ (Matthew 7:13–14; 25:46).

If grace is for all kinds of people, can I tell anyone that Christ will save them? Yes, and you should. The gospel is to be offered freely and sincerely to every person, with the promise that whoever believes in Christ will be saved (John 3:16; Romans 10:13). You do not need to know whether someone is elect to tell them so; God has bound himself to save everyone who comes. There is no one whose background, class, race or past puts them beyond the reach of this grace: the slave and the master, the respectable and the notorious. Tell them that Christ receives sinners, and urge them to come.

For worship. Grace has a birthday. For ages it lay hidden in the heart of God, promised and foreshadowed; then it dawned over a manger, a carpenter’s bench, the roads of Galilee and a hill outside Jerusalem. It came down and shone with the same light on the slave in the kitchen and the master at his table.

verseByVerse.quote: training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Training us. The word is the one for raising a child, the same root as the training in righteousness of 2 Timothy 3:16. And grace is the subject of the verb: not only pardon but a teacher, and the present tense makes it a lifelong school.

Grace does the teaching. Anyone who has heard that too much grace produces loose living should weigh this verse. Paul does not balance grace with law; grace itself does the teaching, and does it better, because a rule can stop a man stealing but cannot make him stop wanting what is not his. Grace goes deeper: it gives a new heart that wants God more than the sin, as the Lord promised when he said he would write his law on his people’s hearts (Jeremiah 31:33).

To renounce ungodliness. To say no to, to reject decisively; it is the same verb used of Peter denying Christ. Ungodliness is irreverence: the root sin, living as if God did not matter.

And worldly passions. Desires belonging to this world in its rebellion against God: lust, greed, pride, envy (1 John 2:15–17). Not desire as such, which God made, but desire bent toward what the world offers in place of him.

Self-controlled, upright, and godly lives. Then the positive: three adverbs, facing three directions: sensibly, the chapter’s word once more, facing inward; justly, facing outward toward others; reverently, facing upward toward God. Between them there is no part of a life left over.

In the present age. This age now: not in retreat from it or when circumstances improve, but on Crete, now, among the liars.

The life grace is shaping. Self-controlled, upright and godly in the present age describes one life that has already been lived. The Son of God was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15); he said no to every worldly passion the devil set before him, dealt justly with every person he met, and lived every hour in communion with his Father. Grace is not training us toward a moral theory. It is conforming us to the image of the Son (Romans 8:29), whose righteousness is already counted to us.

What it does not mean. It does not mean grace makes effort unnecessary. Grace trains, and we learn; grace empowers, and we work (Philippians 2:12–13). Nor does it mean we will be perfect in this age; it means we will grow.

How does grace actually train me? Through the means God has appointed, used in the light of the cross. Grace teaches you through Scripture, which shows you what God loves and hates; through preaching, which applies it; through the Lord’s Supper, which sets Christ’s sacrifice before your eyes; through prayer, where you bring your struggles to him; through the church, where brothers and sisters encourage and correct you; and through providence, including hard things, which God uses to discipline his children for their good (Hebrews 12:10–11). And under all of it, grace trains by changing what you love. The more you see of Christ’s kindness, the less you want what he died to free you from.

What does saying no look like when temptation comes? It looks like a decision made in advance and acted on quickly. Know your particular weak points and plan for them: what you will not look at, where you will not go, what you will do instead. When the temptation comes, do not argue with it; turn from it, as Joseph ran (Genesis 39:12). Pray immediately, even one sentence. Remind yourself of the gospel: I am not a slave to this any more; Christ died to free me from it. Replace it with something good. And if you fall, do not wallow; confess it, receive forgiveness, and get up. Grace that says no to sin also says yes to the sinner who returns.

verseByVerse.quote: waiting for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Waiting for our blessed hope. Grace appeared (v. 11); glory will appear (v. 13); everything in the chapter sits in that gap. Waiting is eager welcoming, not idleness (2 Timothy 4:8), and hope is certain expectation.

The appearing of the glory. The word used for Christ’s return (2 Timothy 4:1). Not merely a glorious appearing, but the appearing of the glory itself (Matthew 25:31). The same word that described grace shining out in verse 11 now describes glory shining out. The first time, he came hidden in flesh; the next time, the glory will be unveiled.

Of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ. Now the crux. The question is whether Paul is naming one person or two: our great God, and our Saviour Jesus Christ; or our great God and Saviour, who is Jesus Christ. In Greek, one article governs both nouns: tou megalou theou kai sōtēros hēmōn Iēsou Christou. By a well-known rule of Greek grammar, often called Granville Sharp’s rule, when one article governs two singular personal nouns that are not proper names, joined by and, both refer to the same person. So Jesus Christ is both our great God and Saviour. Moreover, it is Christ, not the Father, whose appearing the New Testament expects. The same construction appears in 2 Peter 1:1. Other passages also call Jesus God (John 1:1; 20:28; Hebrews 1:8).

The argument closes. The alternation of God our Saviour and Christ our Saviour (1:3, 4; 2:10, 13; 3:4, 6) was an argument being assembled, and here it closes. It also lifts the chapter’s ordinary instructions into a startling light. The slave not pilfering in a Cretan kitchen is adorning the doctrine of God our Saviour (v. 10), and by verse 13 it is plain that this God and Saviour is the man who died for him.

Where Christians differ: is Jesus called God here? Some, including Jehovah’s Witnesses and some older scholars, translate the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ, as referring to two persons, the Father and the Son. (The KJV has that wording too, though its translators may well have meant one person.) This commentary’s view: The grammar, the context, and the New Testament’s consistent expectation of Christ’s (not the Father’s) appearing all support the translation our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ. This is the reading of most modern translations and of the early Greek church fathers, who spoke Greek as their native language. Christ is fully God, equal with the Father, one God in three persons.

What it does not mean. Calling Jesus our great God does not erase the distinction between him and the Father. They are distinct persons, both fully God.

Is our blessed hope a secret rapture before a tribulation? No. Paul names the hope directly: the appearing of the glory of our great God and Saviour. It is one glorious, visible appearing, and that is what believers wait for. Scripture describes Christ’s coming as public, like lightning across the sky (Matthew 24:27), with a shout and a trumpet (1 Thessalonians 4:16), when every eye will see him (Revelation 1:7). At that one coming the dead will be raised, believers will be gathered to meet him, the wicked will be judged, and all things made new. Christians will face trouble before then, as they always have, but their hope is not escape from the world; it is the return of its King. Many sincere believers have been taught a pre-tribulation rapture and share the same longing for Christ; this commentary reads these passages as one coming because each of them is public and loud, and it is no reason for division between brothers.

How do I wait for Christ’s appearing in practice? By living now in a way that would be glad to be interrupted by him. Keep short accounts with God and with others. Hold your possessions loosely, since they will not last. Spend your life on what will: people, the gospel, good works. Pray for his coming, as the church has always prayed, come, Lord Jesus. Let the hope steady you in suffering, because the present age is not the last word. And do not waste energy on date-setting; he has told us to be ready, not to calculate. The best preparation for his appearing is the self-controlled, upright and godly life of verse 12.

For worship. The baby in the manger at Bethlehem is the great God. The man who wept at Lazarus’s tomb is the great God. The one who hung on the cross, mocked and bleeding, is the great God and our Saviour, and the Saviour of a Cretan slave is the God of the universe.
verseByVerse.note: One of the clearest New Testament statements that Jesus is God.

verseByVerse.quote: who gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession who are zealous for good works. Declare these things; exhort and rebuke with all authority. Let no one disregard you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who gave himself for us. Paul does not let the highest statement of Christ’s deity stand for a sentence without the cross under it. The giving is voluntary (Galatians 2:20): not a contribution, but the whole person handed over. “For us” means on our behalf, in our place. This is the heart of the gospel: substitution.

To redeem us from all lawlessness. “Redeem” means to set free by paying a price. It is the language of buying a slave’s freedom (Mark 10:45), and on Crete slaves in the congregation would hear it with longing. All lawlessness means every kind of sin (1 John 3:4), with nothing left unbought. Christ’s death frees us from sin’s penalty (justification) and from its power (sanctification). Psalm 130:8 promised that God himself would redeem Israel from all its iniquities, and here the great God does it.

And to purify for himself a people. Christ died not only to forgive but to make his people clean and holy (Ephesians 5:25–27). For himself: he is not cleaning them for someone else; he wants them.

For his own possession. A treasured possession, echoing God’s words to Israel at Sinai (Exodus 19:5). Paul applies it, without apology, to a scatter of congregations on Crete containing slaves and former liars. The church, made of Jews and Gentiles, is God’s treasured people, the true Israel (1 Peter 2:9–10); Christians differ on whether God also has a future purpose for the Jewish people (Romans 11:25–29), but not on this.

Who are zealous for good works. Eager, passionate. And the order is the whole architecture: he gave himself, he redeemed, he purified, he took possession, and the result is a people eager to do good. The works are not the price of the possession. They are what possession produces (Ephesians 2:10).

In the flow. Verse 14 ends where chapter 1 ended, on good works, but the other way up: the false teachers were unfit for any (1:16), and Christ’s people are zealous for them. These things (v. 15) gathers up the whole chapter.

Declare these things; exhort and rebuke. Announce, encourage, correct: all three are needed. “With all authority” is the note of someone entitled to speak. Titus speaks with the authority of God’s word, not his own.

Let no one disregard you. To look past, to look down on. Timothy was told not to let anyone despise his youth (1 Timothy 4:12); Titus is told not to be ignored. Titus cannot control what people think of him, only whether he gives them grounds (vv. 7–8). A man is disregarded either because he has no authority or because he has given it away.

What it does not mean. All authority does not mean Titus may be harsh or domineering; his authority is the authority of the message.

Did Christ die for everyone, or only for his people? This verse says he gave himself to redeem and purify a people for his own possession, and the purpose was achieved: they are redeemed and are being made zealous for good works. Reformed Christians therefore hold that Christ’s death was designed to save his elect and actually secures their salvation, rather than merely making salvation possible for all and certain for none (John 10:11, 15; Ephesians 5:25). Other evangelicals believe Christ died for every person in the same way. All agree that his death is of infinite worth, sufficient for the whole world, and that the gospel must be offered to everyone. What definite atonement adds is the certainty that the cross did not fail: everyone Christ died for will be his.

If I am not zealous for good works, am I really his? Zeal grows; it does not arrive full-grown. If you trust Christ and want to please him, even feebly, that desire is the beginning of what this verse describes. Ask God to stir it up, and feed it: think often about what Christ gave for you, because zeal is kindled by gratitude, not guilt. Spend time with believers who are eager to do good; zeal is contagious. Start small and practical. But if you feel no desire at all to please God, and are content to be so, take that seriously and go to Christ honestly about it. He does not reject the cold who come to him; he warms them.

For worship. Kings collect treasure they never paid for with themselves. This King gave himself. The great God walked into the slave market of sin, where we stood with nothing to offer, and bought us with his own life, not to set us to work in his fields at a distance but to bring us into his house as his own. He looks at a church of former liars and slaves and calls it his treasured possession, and he means it.
verseByVerse.note: “A people for his own possession” echoes God’s words to Israel at Sinai.

3.title: Heirs of Hope: Conduct in Society and the Gospel's Foundation
3.overview:
The last chapter covers life among unbelieving neighbours (vv. 1–8) and the handling of divisive people (vv. 9–15). Christians are to be good citizens, gentle and courteous to everyone, because they remember what they once were: foolish, enslaved and hateful. What changed them was not their own effort. God our Saviour appeared in kindness and saved us, “not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy”, by the new birth the Spirit gives, so that, justified by grace, we are heirs of eternal life.

Titus is to insist on this free grace so that believers will devote themselves to good works. Pointless controversies are to be avoided, a divisive person warned twice and then left alone, and the travelling teachers sent on well supplied.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — He Saved Us, Not Because of Works
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul turns to how believers live among unbelieving neighbours and rulers, grounding their gentleness in memory: we were once no better. At the centre is one of the Bible’s fullest summaries of salvation, in which Father, Son and Spirit act together.
verseByVerse.theology:
Grace as the Engine of Works

Having excluded even our righteous works from the reason we are saved (v.5), Paul says to insist on that doctrine precisely so that believers devote themselves to good works (v.8). Free grace is not balanced against effort; it drives it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In a province prone to unrest, submission to authorities was the Christian's default posture (v.1; cf. Acts 5:29).

Now: Courtesy toward the ungodly comes from an accurate memory: ‘we ourselves were once’ (v.3).

verseByVerse.quote: Remind them to be submissive to rulers and authorities, to be obedient, to be ready for every good work, to speak evil of no one, to avoid quarreling, to be gentle, and to show perfect courtesy toward all people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Titus 3 moves from life within the church to life in the wider world, and grounds both in the gospel. Believers are to be good citizens, gentle and courteous to everyone (vv. 1–2), because we were once no better than our pagan neighbours (v. 3). What changed us was God’s kindness and mercy, not our works (vv. 4–7), and this saying must be stressed so that believers devote themselves to good works (v. 8). At its centre stands one of the fullest summaries of salvation in the Bible, in which Father, Son and Spirit all act to rescue people who hated one another.

Remind them. “Remind” means keep reminding. Much of a minister’s work is not new information but recollection, and much of the Christian life is remembering what we already know.

To be submissive to rulers and authorities. “Submissive” means ordering themselves under civil government, the teaching of Romans 13:1–7 and 1 Peter 2:13–17: God has instituted government for order and justice. Crete was a Roman province with a reputation for unruliness and rebellion, and the churches probably included Jewish converts (1:10) from communities that resented Rome. A movement suspected of sedition could easily have been crushed.

To be obedient. To obey those in authority, in all that does not require sin (Acts 5:29). Submission is the Christian’s default posture toward legitimate authority; it is not a promise to do whatever he is told.

To be ready for every good work. Good works, the letter’s refrain, appear here as civic usefulness: not just avoiding trouble but contributing to the common good (Jeremiah 29:7; Galatians 6:10). Christians are to be the people a town is glad to have in it.

To speak evil of no one. “Speak evil” means to slander or revile: not even rulers, pagan neighbours or opponents.

To avoid quarrelling, to be gentle. “Avoid quarrelling” is literally to be non-combatant, peaceable, the same requirement as for an overseer (1 Timothy 3:3). “Gentle” resists translation: gracious, reasonable, yielding, the person who does not insist on the last inch of his rights.

And to show perfect courtesy toward all people. Literally showing all meekness toward all people, and the doubled all is the point: every kind of gentleness, toward every kind of person, unbelievers and enemies included. Paul knows how demanding that is, which is why he gives the reason at once (v. 3).

The meekness and gentleness of Christ. The two words for temper in this verse, gentle and meekness, are a pair Paul uses elsewhere of one person: he appealed to the Corinthians by the meekness and gentleness of Christ (2 Corinthians 10:1), and Jesus described himself in the same terms: I am gentle and lowly in heart (Matthew 11:29). The courtesy asked of Cretan believers is Christ’s own temper reproduced in his people: they are to treat a sneering official or a hostile neighbour as their Lord treated Pilate and the soldiers, with a gentleness that is not weakness, because it comes from someone who is not afraid.

How should a Christian speak about politicians he disagrees with? Truthfully, but without contempt. You may say plainly that a policy is unjust, that a leader has lied, or that a law contradicts God’s word; the prophets did. But you may not mock, curse, spread rumours, or speak of anyone as though they were beneath respect. Pray for them by name, as Paul commands (1 Timothy 2:1–2). Before you post or repeat something, ask whether it is true, whether it is kind, and whether you would say it to their face. Paul wrote this under Nero. If courtesy was owed to him, it is owed to the people in office now, of every party.

When must a Christian refuse to obey the government? When it commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands. The apostles refused to stop preaching (Acts 5:29); Daniel kept praying (Daniel 6:10); the Hebrew midwives refused to kill babies (Exodus 1:17). Even then, refuse respectfully and openly, accept the lawful penalty, and do not turn to violence or deceit. In free societies you may also use lawful means to change bad laws: voting, petitioning, speaking, standing for office. What you may not do is treat every law you dislike as an excuse to ignore authority altogether.

For worship. Over every magistrate in Crete, and over Caesar in Rome, stood a higher throne, and the one seated on it had been executed under a Roman governor. Yet he rules as no Caesar ever ruled: a bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench. Because that throne is already occupied, his people need neither fear their rulers nor despise them. They can be gentle with the whole world, as their King has been gentle with them.

verseByVerse.quote: For we ourselves were once foolish, disobedient, led astray, slaves to various passions and pleasures, passing our days in malice and envy, hated by others and hating one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we ourselves were once. The gentleness of verse 2 rests on the memory of verse 3. Not they were, but we ourselves: the Pharisee who was blameless in the righteousness of the law (Philippians 3:6) places himself among the foolish and enslaved without qualification. Humility is the root of gentleness.

Foolish, disobedient, led astray. Seven items trace a descent. “Foolish” means spiritually blind (Ephesians 4:18). “Disobedient” means refusing to be persuaded (1:16). “Led astray” is passive: we did not only wander; we were led, deceived by sin and Satan.

Slaves to various passions and pleasures. Not indulging appetites but owned by them: we thought we were free (Romans 6:16–20).

Passing our days in malice and envy. Not occasional lapses of ill will and jealousy, but the medium a life was lived in.

Hated by others and hating one another. The phrase describes a society, not only individuals: everyone despising and being despised.

An accurate memory. How do you show perfect courtesy to people who are foolish, enslaved and hateful? By remembering that the description is your own. This is Paul’s answer to the superiority a moral religion breeds. Contempt for the ungodly is not defeated by trying harder to be patient; it is defeated by an accurate memory. The Cretan liar is not a different species from the man teaching him. He is a man at a stage his teacher has been through, and the only thing that moved the teacher out of it was the kindness and mercy of God our Saviour.

If the Son sets you free. Paul’s word for our former condition is slavery, and Jesus gave the same diagnosis with its cure. Everyone who practises sin is a slave to sin, he said; and if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed (John 8:34–36). And the hatred at the bottom of the list was met by a love that ran the other way. Christ was hated without a cause (John 15:25), and he loved those who hated him enough to die for them while they were still his enemies (Romans 5:10).

What it does not mean. It does not mean every unbeliever is as bad as they could be in outward behaviour, or that no unbeliever does anything good in a civil sense. It means that, apart from grace, every part of human nature is corrupted by sin and unable to turn to God (Romans 3:10–18; 8:7–8): not that we are as wicked as possible, but that we cannot save ourselves.

If I was raised a Christian, does this describe me? Yes, though it may not feel like it. Paul was raised in the most careful religious home imaginable and still put himself in this list. You may never have been a drunkard or a thief, but the root of this verse is in every human heart: blindness to God, a will that resists him, desires that rule us, envy and pride. A respectable life can hide that from others and from ourselves. The point is not that you must invent a dramatic past, but that you must see your heart as God sees it, and know that you too were saved only by mercy. That is what will keep you gentle with people whose sins are louder than yours.

How do I stop feeling superior to unbelievers? Remember, regularly and specifically, what you were and what you still would be without grace. Remember that the difference between you and them was made by God, not by you (1 Corinthians 4:7). Get to know unbelievers as people, not as categories, and you will often find kindness, honesty and wisdom in them that rebuke you. Pray for them, one face at a time; it is very hard to despise someone you are praying for. And keep looking at the cross, where it becomes clear that Christ died for the ungodly, which includes you.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared, he saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Saviour appeared. Into the mutual hatred of verse 3, something appeared. “Loving kindness” is literally philanthropy. The Greeks praised rulers for their philanthropy; Paul says the true philanthropy is God’s, and he uses it of God toward the very people just described.

Love for mankind in a human face. “Appeared” is the verb of 2:11, and in both places Paul means the coming of Jesus Christ. God’s love for humanity did not stay a disposition in heaven: the Son took our nature and died for people who were foolish, enslaved and hateful. Not a ruler’s gift handed out from a palace, but the King himself coming down into the street. The washing and renewal Paul describes next are the Spirit applying what the Son came to do.

He saved us. The verb describes a completed act, decisive, done. God is the subject; we are the object.

Not because of works. It is not merely works that are ruled out, but works done by us in righteousness: even our righteous ones. The best things we ever did, religious ones included, are excluded from the reason (Ephesians 2:8–9). That is harder for a decent person to hear than for a scoundrel. A salvation we could take some credit for would leave us still in charge and God slightly in our debt; mercy leaves room only for thanks.

But according to his own mercy. The whole cause is on God’s side: mercy is what is shown to the wretched rather than the deserving. Mercy is not the holy God relaxing his law or pretending sin does not matter. He can show mercy to the guilty and still be just, because his Son bore the judgment they deserved (Romans 3:25–26).

By the washing of regeneration. “Regeneration” (palingenesia) is literally genesis again: a new beginning, not a repaired old one. The new birth is a cleansing from sin, as in Ezekiel 36:25–27, where God promises to sprinkle clean water and give a new heart and a new spirit.

And renewal of the Holy Spirit. Probably one event is described two ways: the Spirit washes away sin’s defilement and creates new life. Regeneration is the beginning; renewal continues throughout life (Romans 12:2; 2 Corinthians 4:16). Both are the Spirit’s, and neither is ours.

Where Christians differ: does baptism regenerate? Roman Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and some Anglican traditions take the washing of regeneration to mean baptism, which in their view causes or conveys the new birth. This commentary’s view: The washing is the Spirit’s inner cleansing, which baptism pictures but does not cause. Paul has just said salvation is not by works done by us; if a ritual performed by us caused regeneration, that would contradict it. The new birth is the Spirit’s sovereign work, like the wind (John 3:8), and it is received by faith (Galatians 3:26–27). Baptism is the outward sign of this inward washing, rightly given to those who profess faith. Scripture shows people regenerated before baptism (Acts 10:44–48) and baptised without being regenerated (Acts 8:13, 20–23).

Water and the Spirit. Those who read the verse as baptism also point to John 3:5 and 1 Peter 3:21. But Jesus spoke to Nicodemus before Christian baptism existed, in the language of Ezekiel’s cleansing water; and Peter at once explains that he means not the removal of dirt but an appeal to God for a good conscience. Reformed Christians who baptise the children of believers agree that the water does not itself regenerate; this commentary believes baptism follows repentance and faith (Acts 2:38, 41), and gladly counts them faithful brothers.

What it does not mean. It does not mean regeneration is a reward for faith. Regeneration is God’s work in the dead sinner, which produces faith (John 1:12–13; Ephesians 2:4–5).

If baptism does not save, why be baptised? Because Christ commands it (Matthew 28:19), and because it is the God-given sign of what he has done for you. In baptism you publicly confess your faith, picture your washing from sin, your death and resurrection with Christ (Romans 6:3–4), and your entry into his visible church. It does not make you a Christian, but a Christian who refuses it is disobeying his Lord. If you have trusted Christ and have not been baptised as a believer, speak to your pastor. It is not a reward for spiritual maturity; it is the first step of obedience for every new disciple.

How do I know I have been born again? Not by remembering the moment, which many believers cannot, but by its fruit. The new birth shows itself in faith in Christ, love for God and his people, a new attitude to sin, a desire for his word, and a life that is changing, however slowly (1 John 3:9–10, 14; 5:1). You did not cause it any more than you caused your first birth, but you can see that you are alive. If you trust Christ, you have been born again, because no one comes to Christ unless the Spirit has given him life. And if you are unsure, do not stare inward; look to Christ and ask him for life. He gives the Spirit to those who ask.

In everyday life. Write down, in one sentence, why God saved you. If anything in the sentence is about you, cross it out and try again, and let what is left turn into thanks.

verseByVerse.quote: whom he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that being justified by his grace we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whom he poured out on us richly. Poured out is the language of Pentecost (Acts 2:17), now happening to a scatter of Cretan believers. Richly means lavishly: not rationed by merit or maturity, but poured on the people who were hating one another in verse 3.

Through Jesus Christ our Saviour. Peter explained Pentecost exactly so: being exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you see and hear (Acts 2:33). The rich pouring on Cretan believers is the gift of a risen and enthroned Saviour. And the same Christ is the reason they are heirs. God appointed the Son the heir of all things (Hebrews 1:2), and those joined to him are fellow heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17), so that the inheritance of the next clause is simply his, shared.

The whole Trinity. All three persons are at work in a single sentence: the Father’s kindness (v. 4), the Spirit’s renewal (v. 5), through Christ the Saviour (v. 6). Paul is simply unable to describe salvation without all three of them.

Justified by his grace. “Justified” is the courtroom word: God the Judge declares sinners righteous in his sight, not because they are righteous in themselves (Romans 4:5), freely, by grace. Justification is distinct from regeneration (God’s work in us) but always accompanies it.

We might become heirs. Justified sinners are adopted as God’s children and heirs (Galatians 4:7). An acquitted man walks out of court owing nothing and owning nothing. Paul says we walk out as heirs, which is family language, not legal. The court declares us not guilty and the Father writes us into the will.

According to the hope of eternal life. The same hope named in the letter’s first sentence (1:2), promised by the God who cannot lie: the letter has come round to where it started.

Where Christians differ: is justification a declaration, or a process of becoming righteous? Roman Catholic teaching holds that justification includes the infusion of righteousness, so that a person is made righteous over time and may grow in justification. This commentary’s view: Justification is a once-for-all legal declaration by God that the believing sinner is righteous in his sight, on the basis of Christ’s righteousness imputed to him, received by faith alone. Our sins are counted to Christ, and his righteousness is counted to us (double imputation, 2 Corinthians 5:21). Sanctification, the process of being made holy, follows and is inseparable, but it is not the ground of our acceptance.

Why does it matter whether justification is a declaration or a process? Because it decides where your assurance rests. If you are justified by being made righteous over time, you can never be sure you are righteous enough, and your standing with God rises and falls with your performance. If you are justified by God’s declaration on the ground of Christ’s righteousness, your standing is as secure as Christ’s, complete from the moment you believe, and it cannot be improved or lost. That is not a licence to sin; it is the freedom to grow without fear. Sanctification is real and necessary, but you pursue it as a child already accepted, not as a defendant still awaiting the verdict.

What does it mean that the Spirit was poured out richly on me, when I feel so dry? It means he has been given to you in fullness, whatever you feel. Every believer has the Spirit (Romans 8:9); there is no second class of Christians who have more of him by right. Feelings rise and fall, and seasons of dryness come to the godliest believers, as the psalms show. But the Spirit is still at work in you, keeping you in faith, convicting you of sin, drawing you to Christ. Seek to be filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18) by using the means he uses: the word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper and fellowship. Ask God for a fresh sense of his presence, and he will not give you a stone.

For worship. The Father did not merely pardon us and send us away; he brought us in. His kindness planned it, the Son’s blood and righteousness secured it, and the Spirit, poured out without stint on people who had hated one another, seals it in their hearts. Everything that belongs to Christ is his people’s by inheritance, and the God who cannot lie has promised it.

verseByVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy, and I want you to insist on these things, so that those who have believed in God may be careful to devote themselves to good works. These things are excellent and profitable for people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The saying is trustworthy. This is one of five trustworthy sayings in Paul’s letters to Timothy and Titus (the others are 1 Timothy 1:15; 3:1; 4:9; 2 Timothy 2:11). Here it points back to verses 4–7, perhaps an early creed or hymn.

And I want you to insist on these things. “Insist” (diabebaiousthai) means to speak confidently, to affirm strongly, to maintain. It is the word used of the false teachers’ confident assertions (1 Timothy 1:7); Titus is to press this doctrine as confidently.

So that they devote themselves. This sentence holds the letter together, and its logic runs the opposite way from what we expect. Having excluded works from salvation as thoroughly as language allows, Paul says: insist on that doctrine, so that people will do good works. Free grace is not balanced by a warning about effort; it is the engine of it, and the Spirit poured out richly (v. 6) is its power.

Created in Christ Jesus for this. How can the same gospel exclude works so completely and then produce them so reliably? Because it joins people to Christ. We are his workmanship, Paul told the Ephesians, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them (Ephesians 2:10). Good works are what happens when a person is united to the living Saviour: the more clearly a believer sees that Christ has done everything for him, the more freely Christ works through him.

Careful and devoted. “Be careful” means to give the mind to it: good works are to be planned rather than left to chance. “Devote themselves” is a word for taking the lead in something, sometimes used of practising a trade. Christians are to be in the business of good works.

These things are excellent and profitable for people. Sound doctrine and good works benefit people, believers and the wider society alike, set against the unprofitable controversies of the next verse.

What it does not mean. It does not mean good works earn salvation. They are the fruit and evidence of saving faith (Ephesians 2:10; James 2:17–18). Even the best of them are flawed, and they are accepted because Christ obeyed perfectly in our place and his righteousness is counted as ours (Romans 5:19; Philippians 3:9).

If I am saved by grace alone, why should I work so hard at good works? Because grace has made you a child of God, and children love to please their Father. Because Christ gave himself to make you zealous for good works (2:14), and to neglect them is to neglect the very thing he died for. Because they glorify God and bring others to him (Matthew 5:16). Because they bless people who need them. And because they are the evidence, to yourself and others, that your faith is real. You do not work for your salvation; you work from it, with the energy of someone who has nothing to prove and everything to give.

In everyday life. Most good works are not spontaneous: the meal for a new mother arrives because someone noticed and put it on the calendar. That is Paul’s careful: grace that thinks ahead. There is probably something in your church, workplace or neighbourhood you could take the lead in without waiting to be asked.

For worship. The God who saved us by mercy alone even supplies the good works he then rewards: he planned them, he gives the will and the strength to do them, and on the last day he will say well done. He takes people who were once slaves of their appetites and haters of one another, sets them to work for the good of a whole island, and then, astonishingly, commends them for it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The letter closes with what to avoid (useless controversy and the divisive man), with travel plans that turn into a last lesson about good works, and with grace.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Divisive Man, and the Limit on Patience

The factious man (hairetikos) is warned twice, and then left (v.10): restraint and an end, both.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Controversies are ‘unprofitable’ (v.9), set against good works that are ‘profitable’ (v.8).

Now: The letter's refrain lands on something small: see that two travellers lack nothing (vv.13–14).

verseByVerse.quote: But avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, dissensions, and quarrels about the law, for they are unprofitable and worthless. As for a person who stirs up division, after warning him once and then twice, have nothing more to do with him, knowing that such a person is warped and sinful; he is self-condemned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But avoid foolish controversies. The instruction is to shun them, not to win them (2 Timothy 2:16, 23). Genealogies are speculations built on Old Testament family trees, the same trouble as at Ephesus (1 Timothy 1:4).

Dissensions, and quarrels about the law. These are fights over the law of Moses: the circumcision party’s debates about Jewish rules (1:10, 14).

For they are unprofitable and worthless. The verdict is commercial, set against verse 8’s profitable: every hour spent on quarrels about the law is an hour not spent on cases of urgent need (v. 14).

The law’s quarrels ended at the cross. Why are quarrels about the law of Moses worthless, when the law is God’s own word? Because Christ has fulfilled it. By his death he broke down the dividing wall of hostility between Jew and Gentile, abolishing the law of commandments expressed in ordinances (Ephesians 2:14–15). The circumcision party on Crete were fighting over a wall Christ had already demolished. To reopen those questions as though they decided who belongs to God was not zeal for Scripture but a refusal to let the cross have its say.

In the flow. Verses 10–11 close a circle: the empty talkers had to be silenced (1:10–11); here Titus is told what to do with a man who will not be.

A person who stirs up division. The word (hairetikos) gives us heretic, but at this date it means a factious person, one who forms parties around his own opinions and splits the church. The offence is not primarily wrong belief but the splitting of a congregation.

After warning him once and then twice. Patience and due process: two warnings give a chance to repent (Matthew 18:15–17). Paul is not licensing a quick trigger, and a church that removes someone without clear warnings has not followed this text.

Have nothing more to do with him. There is no third warning: endless patience with a man who is dividing a church is not kindness to the church.

He is self-condemned. He is warped, literally turned inside out. The two warnings are what make him self-condemned: a man who has been told twice, plainly, and persists, has convicted himself out of his own mouth. Titus does not have to judge him. He only has to notice.

What it does not mean. It does not mean anyone who disagrees with church leaders should be excluded. The issue is a divisive spirit that splits the church over foolish and unprofitable matters and refuses correction. And if you are a tender-hearted believer who worries that you have been divisive, your very willingness to be corrected sets you apart from the man Paul describes, who has been warned twice and will not hear.

How do I tell a foolish controversy from a necessary one? Ask whether Scripture speaks clearly to it and whether it touches the gospel or godliness. Titus must rebuke false teachers sharply (1:13) and refute those who contradict sound doctrine (1:9), so defending the truth is not optional. What Paul forbids are arguments built on speculation, things Scripture does not settle, debates pursued for the pleasure of winning, and quarrels that feed curiosity and pride rather than faith and love. A useful test: is this debate making anyone more like Christ, or only more certain they are right? Online, the answer is usually obvious.

What does have nothing more to do with him mean in practice? After two warnings, the church is to put him out of its fellowship, as Jesus and Paul teach elsewhere (Matthew 18:15–17; 1 Corinthians 5:11–13). He should not be allowed to teach, lead or keep spreading division within the church. Believers should not keep debating with him or giving him an audience. But the aim is still repentance: do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother (2 Thessalonians 3:15). Be courteous if you meet him, pray for him, and be ready to welcome him back gladly if he repents. The divisive person is one who will not stop stirring up quarrels, not someone who disagrees honestly.

For worship. The church holds together not because its members win their arguments but because its Lord holds it. Before the cross he prayed that his people would be one, as he and the Father are one, and then he gave his own body to make them one body. He is patient with the quarrelsome, warning before he judges and running to meet every wanderer who turns back. And he guards what he has bought: neither a divisive man in Crete nor the gates of hell themselves will prevail against the church he is building.

verseByVerse.quote: When I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, do your best to come to me at Nicopolis, for I have decided to spend the winter there. Do your best to speed Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way; see that they lack nothing. And let our people learn to devote themselves to good works, so as to help cases of urgent need, and not be unfruitful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Artemas or Tychicus. Artemas appears nowhere else in Scripture. Tychicus was the courier of Ephesians and Colossians (Ephesians 6:21). One of the two will replace Titus in Crete. Paul does not pull a man out of a post without putting someone in it.

Nicopolis. City of victory, probably the city on the west coast of Greece founded by Augustus after Actium: a good base for winter and for mission into Dalmatia, where Titus later went (2 Timothy 4:10).

To spend the winter there. Paul is planning a season’s work, which suggests this letter was written while he was free, probably between a first Roman imprisonment and the chains of 2 Timothy.

Zenas the lawyer and Apollos. Zenas was either a Jewish expert in the law of Moses or a Roman jurist; he is otherwise unknown. Apollos was the eloquent teacher from Alexandria, mighty in the Scriptures (Acts 18:24–28). They were probably carrying this letter. “Speed on their way” is a technical term for providing missionaries with food, money and travel needs (Romans 15:24; 3 John 6).

See that they lack nothing. Travelling teachers depended entirely on the hospitality of churches, and Paul is specific about it in a letter he could have ended three verses earlier.

Let our people learn. Verse 14 turns the errand into a lesson. Good works do not come naturally; the Spirit grows them as believers learn, practise and cultivate them, and devote themselves is the word of verse 8.

So as to help cases of urgent need. Not general benevolence but the specific emergency in front of you, such as Zenas and Apollos passing through. The Cretans, known as idle bellies (1:12), must become known for working and giving.

And not be unfruitful. The word is agricultural: a tree that produces nothing is a failure at being a tree (Matthew 7:17–20). So the letter’s great refrain lands, at the end, on something small and concrete: make sure two travellers have what they need for the journey. That is what devotion to good works looked like on Crete that week.

Fruit from the vine. Paul’s farming word echoes Jesus: I am the vine; you are the branches, he said: whoever abides in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing (John 15:5). The Cretans are told to learn, and it is the learning of branches: staying joined to Christ, drawing on his life, and letting that life come out in practical help wherever the need is urgent.

What it does not mean. It does not mean fruitfulness is measured only by visible results. It is the overflow of a life devoted to Christ, and it often grows slowly and out of sight. A believer who fears he is barren but still clings to Christ is a branch in the vine, and the one who began a good work in him will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6).

How do I learn to devote myself to good works? The way you learn any skill: by practice, by example, and by planning. Watch believers who are good at it and copy them. Look at your week and ask where the urgent needs are: the neighbour after surgery, the family short of money, the missionary on furlough, the student far from home. Set aside money and time in advance, so you are ready when the need arises. Start with what is in front of you rather than waiting for a grand opportunity. And do it as worship, remembering that whatever you do for the least of Christ’s brothers you do for him (Matthew 25:40).

How should my church care for missionaries and visiting preachers? Generously and thoughtfully, so that they lack nothing. Pay their expenses and give a proper gift, not a token. Offer hospitality: a bed, meals, a car, a quiet place to rest. Ask what they actually need, and listen. Pray for them specifically and often, and keep in touch after they leave. Support missionaries over the long term, not only when they visit. John says we ought to support people like these, that we may be fellow workers for the truth (3 John 8). A church that sends its gospel workers on their way well shares in their reward.
verseByVerse.note: Nicopolis was probably the city of that name on the west coast of Greece. Apollos was the gifted teacher from Alexandria.

verseByVerse.quote: All who are with me send greetings to you. Greet those who love us in the faith. Grace be with you all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who love us in the faith. Paul names none of the companions sending greetings, unusually. The letter has been full of people who did not love him: the empty talkers, the men teaching for shameful gain, the divisive man. At the end Paul sends his greeting past them to the ones who love him, and the qualifier in the faith marks the bond: not personal affection merely, but the love of people who hold the same thing.

With you all. “You all” is plural: the letter was addressed to one man but read aloud to the congregations, so the last word goes to the room: to the elders being appointed, the older women told not to gossip, the young wives, the slaves not pilfering, and even, one supposes, the divisive man who still had two warnings coming.

The first word and the last. A letter full of instructions about good works ends, as it began (1:4), with grace, the letter’s argument as well as its frame, and in this letter grace always has a face. It appeared in Jesus Christ; it was paid for when he gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness (2:14); it reaches us through the Spirit poured out through him (3:6). To wish a church grace is to wish it Christ: his favour, his presence and his power with every one of them.

Why does Paul end every letter with grace? Because grace is not only how the Christian life begins but how it continues and how it ends. We are saved by grace, trained by grace, kept by grace, and will be brought home by grace. Every instruction in this letter, to elders, older women, young men, slaves, citizens, assumes it; none of it can be obeyed without it. When Paul says grace be with you all, he is not adding a pleasant sign-off. He is naming the one thing that makes everything else possible, and handing them back to the God who supplies it.

For worship. To an island proverbial for lying, gluttony and disorder, God sent a short letter about decent elders, ordinary duties and grace, and it was enough, because the grace was his. It is the grace of the God who never lies, who appeared in his Son to redeem a people for his own possession and washed them by his Spirit. That grace has never run short. It was enough for Crete, and it is with all his people still.
